editorials.title: Service quality in focus as telecos ring in hikes
editorials.passage: Telecom tariffs in India are back in spotlight with analysts expecting a broad-based increase in the coming months after a two-year pause. Recent stealth price hikes by the country’s two leading telecom operators have fuelled anticipation of a 10-15 percent industry-wide increase. If Bharti Airtel removed its select entry-level prepaid plans with 28-to-60-day validity, effectively raising the price of some of its lower-end offerings earlier this month, Reliance Jio followed suit with a similar move. While it retained its entry-level data plan intact, it reintroduced Jio Prime membership at a one-time fee of ₹300. This price protection guarantee till September 2027, in a way, signals that a hike is likely in the next six months, according to brokerage Motilal Oswal Financial Services. Another factor prompting speculation over higher tariffs is that price hikes in India often follow a 2-3 year cycle and the last such increase occurred in July 2024.Raised rates in the past have led to higher average per-user revenues of about ₹15-20 a month even though operators lose subscribers. Data from the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India shows that the three leading operators—Jio, Airtel and Vodafone—together shed 23.14 million subscribers between June and September of 2024 following the last round of hikes. Indian customers are now moving away from being price-sensitive to value-sensitive decisions, while operators are shifting focus from infrastructure rollouts to revenue generation. This is essential given that India is the world’s second-largest telecom market by subscriber base. Of the total 1.348 billion connections, the broadband subscriber base alone surged past 1.08 billion owing to rising smartphone use, affordable tariffs and growing demand for high-speed connectivity in both urban and rural areas..Even though teledensity stood at over 90 percent, expanding connectivity and improving service quality in rural and remote areas remain a challenge. Call drops continue to be a major problem, with operators facing intense pressure to improve network reliability and deliver uninterrupted data services. At the same time, adoption of next-generation technologies such as internet-of-things and Cloud-based communications has increased cybersecurity risks. All of this means telecom companies must strengthen network security and safeguard customer data at all costs. editorials.title: More needed than pact to address social media addiction among kids
editorials.passage: In a landmark deal with potentially far-reaching beneficial impact on children, Meta Platforms on Wednesday agreed to pay up to $18 billion over the next 10 years and strictly limit how teenagers use Facebook and Instagram. The agreement with almost all US states followed a trial over allegations that Meta’s products were harmful as its social media platforms are designed to get children addicted. The agreement, which cut short multiple lawsuits, requires Meta to disable most push-notifications to teenagers during school hours and enhance measures to prevent them from accessing age-restricted content. It is hoped that such limits can be tightened further if other social media platforms like YouTube and Snapchat adopt similar terms to help tackle growing social media addiction among youngsters.The accord is being seen as an unprecedented template to resolve thousands of other lawsuits against social media companies. Not just the US, governments across the world are trying to grapple with the issue. Australia, Indonesia, Malaysia and Brazil have banned or mandated strict parental control for social media use by children under 16; the UK is considering a similar move. Several Indian states are talking along the same line..Social media addiction is known to cause a range of problems among the young, particularly mental health issues (depression and anxiety, low self-esteem, sleep disruption); brain and cognitive effects (shortened attention span and reduced grey matter, particularly affecting parts of the brain linked to self-control and decision-making); withdrawal symptoms when staying offline (social isolation, lower productivity and strain in relationships)—all contributing to mental health issues. Many of these have ended tragically in suicides in India and elsewhere—which is why the Wednesday accord is viewed as a much-welcome development.However, addressing these problems requires much more than what the deal promises. Experts—including influential social and cultural psychologist Jonathan Haidt—have pointed out that Meta’s still-running AI-powered recommendation engine continues to maximise engagement with harmful content. This brings into play the importance of responsible parenting, robust counselling (in academic institutions and outside) and governmental controls that pay close attention to the cultural contexts of countries and communities. The social, mental and neurological well-being of children is at stake. editorials.title: Quick Take | For cooler homes
editorials.passage: As Italy faces the summer’s most intense heatwave this weekend, fresh number-crunching by a Spanish health research institute reveals 35,000 more deaths than usual during Europe’s four record-breaking heatwaves this year. Excess mortality in Germany, France and Spain alone crossed 25,000, according to the provisional estimate. Other numbers from the International Energy Agency set the context: only one in four European households had air-conditioning in 2025, compared to nine out of 10 in Japan and the US; the comparable number for India is closer to one in 20. While this is music to the ears of AC salespeople, the longer-term planning for all countries must involve serious rethinking of how we build houses. editorials.title: Apocalypse now
editorials.passage:
It rained last Thursday in London after two months of dry, sunny weather that English meteorologists describe as “fine”. This used to puzzle me once because summers in India featured months of blazing, rainless heat that were anything but fine. I learnt that fine weather meant the sunny breaks in the cloudy, garden-sprinkler climate that made Britain a fat, fertile island and mildly depressed its people.

This summer might change that. In the month that I’ve been here, the evidence of drought is everywhere; brown lawns, dry hedgerows, hosepipe bans, cheap fans, half-naked, buxom Englishmen and irritable double-decker drivers stewing in their plexiglass cubicles. The BBC’s report on the drought opened with “Hyde Park looks more like the Serengeti and the green belt has turned yellow.” We drove from Brighton to London and the downs and wealds in between had been reduced to scrub. We stopped for lunch at a pub in Hambledon, the birthplace of cricket’s early laws, and the Broadhalfpenny Down that used to be Hambledon Cricket Club’s home ground was a sere, brown bowl sloping away from its mottled square.

England is living through a textbook case of climate change. A high pressure dome has settled over the country, trapping heat below it and preventing adjacent rain-bearing winds from dispersing the heat. The jet stream, best thought of as a high altitude stream of air, that in normal years would push the dome of heat away, is now too sluggish to do its job. The temperature difference between the equator and the poles that gave the jet stream its momentum has shrunk because polar ice caps have been heating up faster than the rest of the planet. The result is that what in earlier years would have been a spell of glorious sunshine that peaked at 28ºCelsius is now a properly Indian summer that threatens 40ºC.

The political Right in England, as elsewhere in the world, opposes any policy that might mitigate climate change. Politicians like Kemi Badenoch, the leader of the Opposition, and Richard Tice, the leader of an extreme Right party, have made opposing Net Zero, till recently a Conservative Party goal, their political credo. They argue that given the scale of Asian emissions, Britain achieving Net Zero would make no difference to global warming.

This is an example of how infantilised politics in the West has become; Western countries like Britain and the United States of America have decided that blaming Daddy China for current emissions lets them free ride on that country’s massive investment in clean renewable energy sources. Even a decade ago, there used to be an acknowledgment of the West’s responsibility for historical emissions and a recognition that tackling global warming needed a global compact negotiated in good faith.

That’s gone now. The only national politician in England who believes in Net Zero is Edward Miliband, so Andy Burnham has made him foreign secretary to make sure he can’t do anything about it. Miliband couldn’t become chancellor because Burnham came to believe he would spook the bond markets with his incendiary ecological beliefs. Tice’s view that the English should “adapt” to climate change by enjoying England’s Mediterranean summers and its Home County vineyards represents Britain’s political consensus. He says out loud what Labour’s Centrist leadership is too embarrassed to own up to. The trouble is that global warming won’t be a gradual process that benignly turns the Isle of Wight into Ibiza even in countries located in temperate latitudes. Raging wildfires of the sort that have broken out in France, Spain, even Wales are the likelier consequences.

A preview of the apocalypse that lies in wait for a procrastinating world made the headlines midweek when a glacier collapse in Tibet resulted in cascading floods that killed hundreds of people. The world’s grandest mountain ranges — the Alps, the Andes, the Himalayas — are heating up faster than the lowlands they look over. As glacier ice warms up, the chances of a glacier fracturing and releasing gigantic quantities of ice, rubble, mud and water into river systems unable to contain them rise. This seems to have happened on the Nepal-China border.

A sheared-off glacier set off a tsunami of mud and water that swallowed river valleys and swept away pilgrim towns. More than five hundred people are confirmed dead and nearly three thousand are missing. Given global warming, experts warn that catastrophic events like this one are likely to recur.

What is terrifying is that these receding, collapsing glaciers presage an even more existential threat to life in South Asia, the most densely-populated region in the world. A majority of the two billion people who live there depend on perennial, glacier-fed Himalayan rivers for drinking water, irrigation and hydroelectric power, for life and livelihood. Pakistan and North India are already amongst the most heat- and water-stressed regions in the world. It won’t take much for their summers to become literally unbearable as wet bulb temperatures push the limits of the human body’s tolerance.

A global geopolitics that abandons collective action on climate change in the name of national self-interest or inevitability is dabbling in a suicidal form of knowingness. First, even if the world is past the point where it can limit the post-industrial rise in global temperatures to less than two degrees, individual countries still need concerted global action to slow the rate of the rise and to mitigate the disasters that global warming will bring in its train. Second, what starts in, say, South Asia won’t stay in South Asia. The South Asian diaspora, already by some estimates the largest in the world, will become exponentially larger if the polycrisis, the intersecting economic, military and ecological crises that define our times, metastasizes on account of unregulated warming. For the West to do everything it can to keep the South livable would be an act of enlightened self-interest.

That said, the principal responsibility for slowing and mitigating climate change in South Asia vests in South Asian states. Bangladesh has led the way in climate adaptation. Its community-based cyclone warning systems and shelters are exemplary achievements for a poor country. India, the largest country in the region, has invested relatively heavily in renewable energy. But its government’s willingness to deregulate the country’s forests and natural resources to favour crony conglomerates, its unwillingness to rein in the construction and transport lobbies that have made India’s cities polluted hellholes, its addiction to sectarian politics and its near-uniformly hostile relations with its subcontinental neighbours make Indian environmental leadership in South Asia a dangerously remote prospect.

editorials.title: PM Modi, Amit Shah mark Raksha Bandhan with children amid BJP unease over youth protests
editorials.passage:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his de facto number two, the Union home minister, Amit Shah, both celebrated Raksha Bandhan with children on Friday. However, the similarities ended there. The two leaders marked the festival separately, with Modi hosting schoolgirls at his official residence, 7 Lok Kalyan Marg in Delhi, and Shah celebrating in his Lok Sabha constituency, Gandhinagar, with girls living with Type 1 diabetes. The girls tied rakhis on Shah as part of the Centre’s initiative to provide free insulin to children up to 18 years of age diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes. The disease requires lifelong insulin injections, imposing a heavy financial burden on economically weaker families. Both Modi and Shah posted photographs of their respective events on X. Shah hailed the free-insulin initiative as a “visionary” step by the Modi government, claiming that even several developed countries were still struggling to implement such a scheme. Modi’s post featured photographs of candid moments with the children — images that appeared designed to reinforce his political messaging about his popularity among youngsters. The parallel celebrations came amid speculation over differences within the top leadership of the Bharatiya Janata Party on the handling of the recent Gen Z protests. The growing unrest among the youth has clearly triggered unease in sections of the ruling party.

The tough stand adopted by the Communist Party of India (Marxist) veteran and incumbent leader of Opposition, Pinarayi Vijayan, over the Communist Party of India’s demand for the post of deputy leader of Opposition in the Kerala assembly has reached a deadlock. The CPI(M) general-secretary, MA Baby, has endorsed Vijayan’s stand while the Kerala CPI leadership appears intent on continuing to pressure the CPI(M).

Speculation is rife that Vijayan would step down from office and make way for the former finance minister, KN Balagopal, which could see the CPI MLA, K Rajan, being anointed as the deputy leader of the Opposition. The CPI, which is the second largest party in the Left Democratic Front, believes it has the right to demand the deputy leader post. But Vijayan is in no mood to relent.

The Union tribal affairs minister, Jual Oram, has accused some of his party leaders who joined the saffron party after switching loyalties of running a sustained campaign to damage his reputation and engineer his removal from the Union cabinet. Oram’s remark came after one of his political associates, Rakesh Paswan, was arrested in Bihar on August 26 for allegedly providing shelter to armed criminals at the government-run Circuit House at Rourkela. Paswan had been absconding for 11 days. Although Oram has made it clear that the law should take its own course, sections of the local media are dragging him into the case.

Enraged by such reports, the six-time member of Parliament from Sundergarh said some people were conspiring to defame him. According to Oram, these leaders hope to secure a cabinet berth if he were dropped. Oram had earlier announced that he would not contest elections again. However, he now says that in the prevailing circumstances he has decided to contest the 2029 general elections. Sources said Oram was apparently referring to the newly elected Rajya Sabha member, Dilip Ray, who hails from Rourkela in Sundergarh district.

Rumours has it that a Bihar minister was beaten with a sandal by a female employee of a luxury hotel in Delhi after he allegedly misbehaved with her. Sources in the Delhi police, however, remained tight-lipped about the posts over the ‘chappal kand ’ that went viral on social media, saying there was no official complaint regarding the incident. The reported incident apparently took place last month when the minister was in Delhi to attend a seminar. The word on the grapevine is that the politician had made some lewd remarks that angered the employee, prompting her to beat him with a sandal. Senior employees of the hotel rushed to the scene and the matter was subsequently ‘resolved’ after the man revealed his identity.

Years ago, when a BJP MP asked a Congress counterpart what religious knowledge he had gained from studying at a Christian school, the latter recited the Serenity Prayer: “O God, give us the serenity to accept what cannot be changed, the courage to change what can be changed, and the wisdom to know the one from the other.” After the recent organisational changes, the BJP leader found himself left out. When the Congress MP — a former Union minister — asked him how things were going, the BJP leader simply folded his hands, looked up at the sky and said, “Christian prayer”.

editorials.title: Not for all: Editorial on Vishwa Hindu Parishad diktat to reshape Durga Puja in Bengal
editorials.passage:
If the Bharatiya Janata Party comes to power, can the Vishwa Hindu Parishad be far behind? The VHP is supposed to be a non-political body with no member elected to government office. Yet it lays down religious rules on all occasions when its sibling in the sangh parivar is in government. The Durga Puja in West Bengal has provided it with a spacious field on which to pronounce its diktat. The sarbojanin Durga Puja has long been the high point of Bengal’s festivals, which artists and makers of different kinds employ their highest skills to produce. They come from all religious communities, major and minor, just as the organisers of quite a few Pujas do. Durga Puja not only engages everybody who can contribute to its creation but also welcomes all visitors to its pandals . The joy of sharing is uppermost during this festival; it is religious, cultural and social all together. Everyone can have the thrill of listening to the drumbeats, of discovering new forms of creativity and aesthetic excellence at the different venues — from the pandals themselves to the lights, images and decorations. Various themes give the Pujas a social edge while religious rituals are carried on at the centre.

The VHP, however, has decided to change the nature of the festival. Speaking at a meeting held with the Forum for Durgotsav, which represents around 500 major Pujas in Calcutta, and with other organisers, VHP members made clear that Durga Puja should be organised and executed by “ sanatani Hindus” alone. The “culture, emotion and enthusiasm” of any religion must be protected and borne by members of that religion, it said. People of other religions should be confined to visiting pandals . That is, they should have no part in the organisation. Yet the convention of Durga Puja is to include all interested residents of a locality irrespective of their religion. The VHP’s diktat is disruptive of that sense of brotherhood and peaceful — on this occasion, joyful — coexistence. It sabotages the idea of sarbojanin — ‘for all’.

Not content with this instruction, the VHP added that traditional religious customs and rituals should be strictly followed. It will reward organisers for — presumably correct — religious rituals and the best priest. Does that mean that Durga Puja in Bengal was hitherto being conducted without regard for religious rules? The VHP will kindly allow non-vegetarian stalls outside the venue if all within is satvik — pure and spiritual. Images should have no distortions, should be properly clad, and pandals should not offend Hindu sentiments. Evidently, there should be no experiment with the former and the latter shall not depict edifices of any other religion. The VHP will disapprove.

But the spirit of the Durga Puja festival is dynamic, creative and inclusive; can its joy be killed by rigidity in the name of protecting the religion? The uniqueness of the festival and its aesthetic power put it on the UNESCO’s representative list of Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. It brings people together; it does not drive them apart. Its sarbojanin spirit is the secret of its magic.

editorials.title: Letters to the editor: Jaipur Nagar Nigam switches to ‘Hinglish’ for citizens’ ease
editorials.passage:
Sir — Jaipur Nagar Nigam has achieved something that seems anathema to most government departments — being citizen-friendly. The JNN website has switched from officialese to ‘Hinglish’ — complaint categories include “Colony ke bahar ka dustbin khali karna hai”, “Helper kuda nhi uthata hai”, “Road par se malva hatwa do” and so on — to ensure that those trying to using the website have no trouble translating English jargons. Plain language should become a requirement across public administration. Citizens turn to the government during stressful moments; language should not add to their worries.

Sir — Dolly Parton’s death closes a remarkable chapter in music. Her songs survived changing fashions because they spoke plainly about desire, poverty, work and separation. “Jolene” captured insecurity without blaming another woman, while “Coat of many colours” turned childhood hardship into a lesson about dignity. “I will always love you” showed that affection could remain after a professional partnership ended. Parton understood feelings and expressed them in language ordinary listeners could recognise. That clarity explains why her music travelled internationally.

Sir — Few women in country music possessed Dolly Parton’s control over their careers. She left Porter Wagoner’s television programme when independence became necessary, then crossed into popular music and films on her own terms. She also retained rights to her songs, protecting the work that created her reputation. Such decisions required discipline in an industry that routinely underestimated female performers. Parton’s success offers a lesson: artistic talent is not enough; financial judgement, firm boundaries and the confidence to choose a different path are the skills needed to succeed.

D.P. Bhattacharya, Calcutta

Sir — The wigs, rhinestones and theatrical make-up were deliberate choices made by Dolly Parton. She used humour to answer those who treated her appearance as evidence of limited intelligence.

Sir — The article, “Tamed tongue” (Aug 28), was thought-provoking. It made me think of another aspect of language. Using masculine words as universal terms in speech and writing can affect readers’ and listeners’ imagine. Psychological research indicates that generic forms such as ‘he’ or ‘mankind’ often produce male mental images rather than inclusive ones. Neutral alternatives such as ‘they’, ‘humanity’, ‘police officer’ and ‘chairperson’ make it easier to picture women in public roles. This is not grammatical fussiness. Repeated wording influences assumptions about who belongs in authority, science or skilled work. Inclusive language gives sentences accuracy when the people being described are not men.

Sir — Women are facing linguistic disadvantages in newer ways with each passing day. Research from Cornell University showed that translation using Artificial Intelligence can insert sexism into literature that contained none. A study involving Bengali and other languages with gender-neutral pronouns found that AI systems often rendered doctors as he, nurses as she, men as workers and women as cooks when translating texts — an Odia cook becoming a she is one instance. These errors matter because translated texts are read by a readership unaware of the nuances of the original. Many vernacular languages are more egalitarian than English. But in the absence of humans eyes, vernacular texts are succumbing to the sexism of English language.

editorials.title: CSR: Where does the money go?
editorials.passage:
In July 2026, a report delivered a triumphant headline: ‘India Inc’s corporate social responsibility (CSR) spending hit a record ₹40,794 crore in 2024-25, up 17 per cent on the year before’. More companies are giving than ever, and a larger share of the money is going straight into projects rather than into government funds. On the surface, a policy experiment is working.

Yet a record number only measures how much was spent, not whom it reached. That is the question worth asking, since the fund now is large enough to matter.

India is one of very few countries to make corporate charity a legal duty. Under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013, any company with a net worth of ₹500 crore or more, a turnover of ₹1,000 crore or more, or net profit of ₹5 crore or more must spend at least 2 per cent of its average net profit over the previous three years on approved social causes, from education and health to rural development and the environment.

Nearly 30,000 firms now spend under the rule. But no central plan directs the money. Each company picks its own causes, its own projects and, crucially, its own locations. Multiply those thousands of separate decisions across a decade and a pattern takes shape, and the pattern is not the one the law’s drafters might have hoped for.

The money follows income, not need. Chart 1 makes this plain. Each bubble is a State; its position from left to right shows income per person, and its height shows CSR received per person (Ministry of Corporate Affairs database). If giving followed need, the richer States on the right would receive less per head, and the bubbles would slope downward.

They do the opposite. The dashed line rising from bottom-left to top-right is the trend, and almost every large State sits along it. In 2024-25 the link between a State’s wealth and its CSR per person was strong, with a correlation of +0.71, and it has stayed strong for 11 years running.

The consequences are stark at the extremes. Delhi received roughly ₹1,243 per person and sits high in the “over-served” zone. Bihar, among the poorest States in the country, received about ₹35 a head, pinned to the bottom-left corner. Uttar Pradesh, at ₹92, and West Bengal, at ₹108, are not far above it. These are three of India’s largest and least prosperous populations, and they draw some of the thinnest support.

If we narrow the lens to a single sector, the same logic hardens. Education is the single biggest CSR cause, absorbing about 34 per cent of all spending in 2024-25. Chart 2 plots each State’s SDG-4 (quality education) score against how much education CSR it receives per person. Bihar has the weakest education outcomes in the country (SDG-4 (quality education) score of 32 — worst in India). In 2023-24, it received about ₹4 per person for education. Delhi, the top on outcomes (SDG-4 score of 85 — highest in the country), got about ₹286, seventy times more.

And education is no outlier. Together with health, it accounts for roughly 56 per cent of all CSR, and both causes lean towards the States already doing best. When corporate money piles up where public provision is already strongest, it widens the gaps it was meant to close.

The cause is not corporate indifference. Every firm’s logic is sound on its own terms: they spend near their plants and offices, invest in the communities they draw workers and goodwill from, and back the causes they know how to run. Since industry concentrates in the richer States, so does the money. The distortion is not the work of any villain; it is the aggregate of thousands of individually reasonable decisions, none of which was ever asked to consider the national map.

That is exactly why this is a question of design rather than conscience. And the concentration is a habit, not a hard limit. When the pandemic struck, CSR pivoted within weeks, pouring into health and relief through 2020-21. Once the emergency eased, giving settled back into its familiar grooves. Corporate India can plainly move money to acute need when it chooses to. Left alone, its choices simply point elsewhere.

The remedy need not be heavy-handed, and it should not be. India already has the scaffolding. NITI Aayog’s aspirational-districts programme maps the country’s most under-served pockets with hard data. The most direct nudge would be to match private rupees spent in those districts with public ones, so that a company’s giving stretches furthest where it is scarcest.

Gentler tools point the same way: recognition for firms that invest in the hardest places, or lighter compliance for money that reaches the bottom of the development ladder.

None of this dictates where a company must spend. It rewards the choice the mandate was always meant to encourage. Sharper disclosure would help too, since today we can see where the money goes but almost nothing about what it achieves.

The architects of Section 135 got the hard part right. They built a large, durable stream of development finance and made corporate India a genuine partner in it. The unfinished task is the one this year’s headline glides past: not how much is given, but where. A decade in, the fair question for policymakers and boardrooms alike is whether we are willing to send the money somewhere harder.

The writer is Lead Economist and Head of Center of Data for Economic Decision-making (CoDED) at Pahlé India Foundation

Published on August 29, 2026

editorials.title: What’s wrong in using AI to write articles, asks ChatGPT
editorials.passage:
The Wall Street Journal recently published an oped article written by a regular contributor using AI. That set off a global debate on whether opinion-makers should use Artificial Intelligence (AI) to write articles. Our columnist TCA Srinivasa Raghavan asked ChatGPT to weigh in on the matter in the form of a 650 word article, written in his style. Here’s the output:

There is a curious new anxiety doing the rounds in newspaper offices: that artificial intelligence might write articles.

This is apparently a bad thing.

I have never quite understood why.

Newspapers have spent decades getting machines to do almost everything except write the article. They use computers to receive copy, edit it, transmit it, lay it out, print it and distribute it. They use software to count words, check spelling, track readership and tell editors which stories people are reading.

But the moment somebody suggests that a machine might help write the words, journalists suddenly discover the sanctity of human creativity.

This is rather like railway employees objecting to electric trains because steam locomotives have souls.

The first objection is that AI cannot write as well as a good journalist.

Quite right. Neither can most journalists.

The second is that AI will eventually replace journalists. Possibly. But that is not an argument against using it. It is an argument for becoming better at journalism. At least in principle.

There is an important distinction here: between reporting and writing.

Reporting is what makes journalism journalism. Finding something out, persuading somebody to talk, discovering the document nobody else has seen, noticing that two apparently unrelated facts are related, understanding the significance of a number and asking the question everybody else was too lazy to ask — these are human activities.

Writing the resulting 600 words is not necessarily one of them.

So why should the first draft of an article be sacred? It isn’t.

What matters is whether the article is true, useful and interesting.

This is where the argument against AI becomes particularly odd. Nobody seriously proposes that journalists should publish whatever they write without editing. Every decent newspaper has layers of checking between the reporter and the reader.

The answer to all these problems is the same: editing.

The real danger is not that AI will write newspaper stories. The real danger is that newspapers will use AI badly.

Consider a reporter receiving a 400-page government report. Somebody has to read it, search it, extract the tables, compare them with last year’s numbers and identify what has changed.

AI can do much of that donkey work in minutes. That does not mean the machine has written the story. It means the journalist has been given something journalists desperately need: time.

A good reporter should spend less time copying numbers from page 137 of a PDF and more time asking why those numbers have changed.

AI can produce the routine stuff quickly and consistently. That leaves human beings to do the difficult stuff.

Of course there is a catch. Editors will have to edit. This sounds obvious, but nobody seems to have thought it through.

If AI produces a draft, somebody has to decide whether it is good enough. Somebody has to check the facts. Somebody has to understand the subject. Somebody has to know what has been omitted.

In other words, AI does not eliminate the need for editors. It makes good editors more important.

And perhaps that is what really frightens people.

Nobody is suggesting that the editorial page should be written by a toaster. But a 250-word report on a routine corporate earnings announcement does not acquire moral value merely because a human being typed it.

The reader wants to know what happened. The reader does not care whether the first draft was produced by an intern, a sub-editor, a reporter sitting in a cab or a large language model sitting in a data centre somewhere. The reader cares whether it is right. That, ultimately, is the test newspapers should apply.

Not: Was this written by AI? But: Is this good journalism?

If the answer is yes, refusing to publish it because a machine helped produce it would be rather like refusing to use a calculator because arithmetic should be done by hand.

There is a word for that. Stupid.

Published on August 29, 2026

editorials.title: Mayors are the big winners in Burnham’s devolution drive. So what happens to areas without mayors?
editorials.passage:
A part from the joyous hyperactivity that comes with suddenly making it to No 10, there are good reasons why Andy Burnham seems to be a prime minister in a hurry. If he decides that his first term is going to run to its maximum length, he has three years, which is a maddening time-frame: too long for him to just tinker here and there, set out his long-term vision and then ask the electorate for permission to do more, but probably too short to start and finish many of his key projects. His chosen solution, it seems, is a mixture of the strategies he would use for each approach, which includes running at some issues at breakneck pace.

So it is with his specialist subject: devolution for England. The huge changes now afoot actually began under Keir Starmer, with the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act passed earlier this year. Areas that previously had two tiers of local government will see them replaced with new unitary councils. But the most historic move centres on regional mayors – what the government calls “strategic authorities” – and a shift that the Whitehall PR machine is hyping up as a “fundamental rewiring of the way our country works, surrendering power that for too long has been held in Westminster and Whitehall”. In principle, this is unquestionably worth celebrating. But it also gives rise to a whole range of increasingly urgent and awkward questions.

One change became clear earlier this year, and now looks like it will be turbocharged . By April 2027, regional and metro mayors will be able to keep as-yet-unspecified quantities of the business rates generated in their areas, and from the following year onwards, they will retain a share – also yet to be announced, presumably because the Treasury and No 10 North are wrestling with it – of local income taxreceipts.

These revenue streams will replace existing Whitehall grants rather than being additional money. But Burnham’s announcements have, among the more established and confident mayors, triggered visions of even greater liberation from Westminster and Whitehall, and possible command of schools, GP services, childcare and much more. There are also welcome predictions of loans being taken out against mayoral authorities’ projected income to fund long-overdue projects, most promisingly in housing and public transport.

England’s 14 regional and metro mayors are right to see a growing opportunity for a civic political renaissance. Burnham and his people are equally correct in their conviction that improving public services and infrastructure, and firing up growth, demands a leading role for these mayors. But whatever the PM’s insistence that he intends to foster “good growth in every postcode”, the core of the vision is undeniably city-based. As the London School of Economics’ local government expert Tony Travers told me last week: “The whole idea of this version of economic change, which is very embedded, is that the only way to make the economies of city regions work is by letting the central part of the city develop fast, and hope that people will commute in and out to take advantage of it.”

And at that point, we should pause for thought. I write this from Somerset, which sits just outside the West of England mayoral combined authority (containing Bristol, South Gloucestershire, and Bath and North East Somerset) and therefore has no regional leader, nor yet plays any part in a strategic authority. Together with its neighbouring county of Wiltshire, it contains the sort of places that almost no one talks about: towns ringed by countryside or on the coast – Melksham, Bridgwater, Calne, Minehead , Trowbridge – that have experienced serious decline, and have been denied a voice for far too long.

Too many places, in fact, are now years behind parts of the country whose devolution journeys began a long time ago. The best thing to be by far is an established mayoral strategic authority – which, according to a House of Commons library briefing , qualify for the widest range of powers and integrated multi-year funding settlements, and include Greater London, Greater Manchester, the Liverpool city region, the West Midlands and such recently elevated territories as Cambridgeshire and Peterborough and the aforementioned West of England.

A second tier is reserved for such “mayoral strategic authorities” as Tees Valley, Greater Lincolnshire – led by Reform UK’s Andrea Jenkyns – and Hull and East Yorkshire, which have to wait at least 18 months after their foundation to join the top rank, and have more restricted or ringfenced funding. They will probably soon include areas that the government is still in the arduous process of getting on board, including Kent and Medway, and “Wessex”: a giant territory that will include Wiltshire , Dorset, Bournemouth and – oh joy! – Somerset. And beneath them, you find foundation authorities such as Lancashire and Devon and Torbay, which have no elected mayor yet and are run by local politicians.

When we spoke, Travers asked me a rhetorical question: “What happens to all the places that are not in high-performing areas that can build up their tax base?” We do not really know the answer yet, because so many of those areas are barely on the first devolutionary rung. Stoke-on-Trent, for instance, which needs every shred of help and local empowerment it can get, only took its first steps to joining a foundation authority in March this year. Cornwall, to which the same applies in spades, finally agreed to become a single-foundation authority at the end of last month. The story of devolution up to now, all told, is replete with delays and procrastination: in late 2025, for instance, the Starmer government postponed mayoral elections in Greater Essex, Sussex and Brighton, Hampshire and the Solent, and Norfolk and Suffolk from 2026 until 2028.

And then everything changed. On 31 July, the new government put out a statement titled Re-wiring The State, setting out its ambition to make central government “smaller and more strategic” and “to ensure every area in England has, or is in the process of establishing, a strategic authority by the end of 2027, with strategic authorities in place everywhere by the end of 2028”. Given that most councils and public services are hopelessly cash-strapped and overburdened, that is a remarkable timetable, particularly in the midst of other devolution headaches. The weekend brought news that plans for new, larger police forces are being delayed because their proposed boundaries don’t match up with those of some mayoral authorities. The reports also mentioned the PM’s unwieldy-looking proposals for reconfigured fire and rescue services and integrated care boards to fit with devolution areas in the same way: there are slight shades of lines and shapes being drawn on maps, and messy reality being hurriedly squeezed into them.

There is another potential problem: the whole programme threatens a system with not nearly enough accountability. Even if an elected mayor is in place – and remember, some of them will probably be from Reform, with all that may entail – proper scrutiny will be in short supply. The only area with an elected assembly that can properly monitor the mayor will still be London: the rest will have “scrutiny committees” that do not sound very convincing at all.

Note also a plain fact about those established, pre-eminent mayoral strategic authorities: most of them are in the north of England and the Midlands, which might avenge years of southern dominance, but seems to threaten answering one story of unfairness with another. As a resident of the south-west, I know we have an immense amount to contribute to the devolution drive, which needs to feed ideas upwards to Whitehall as well as down from central government to the social grassroots. If the past 15 years have taught us anything, it is that the worst thing to be, politically speaking, is left behind: as fast as he and his senior mayoral mates move, Burnham has to be sure that speed and zeal do not have very damaging consequences, and that he takes absolutely all of us with him.

John Harris is a Guardian columnist

editorials.title: Trump’s ‘economic D-day’ against Iran risks driving the stakes even higher
editorials.passage:
D onald Trump has found a new way to promise victory over Iran. After months of war have failed to force Iran’s capitulation or collapse, his administration has unveiled what the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, calls Operation Economic Outcast: an effort to cut it off from what remains of the global economy and threaten foreign governments, banks and companies with sanctions if they continue doing business with Tehran.

There is no question that Iran is vulnerable. Its economy has been battered by years of sanctions, war and a months-long US naval blockade. Iranian officials acknowledge that oil exports and access to foreign currency have been severely constrained. Ordinary Iranians are already enduring high inflation, currency depreciation and worsening living standards. Further economic strangulation will inflict significant additional hardship.

Iran also wants an end to the war. Its president, Masoud Pezeshkian, has said it should seek peace while it can still negotiate from a position of “power and dignity”. But Iran needing a deal is not the same as Iran preparing to surrender. That distinction has repeatedly eluded Trump in formulating his Iran policy: ramping up pressure is not the same as having a strategy. Iran gets a move too.

Indeed, Iranian officials increasingly suggest this strategy has the opposite effect than what was intended. Each successive escalation, in their telling, demonstrates why Iran relinquishing its remaining leverage would simply leave it vulnerable to the next round of US pressure. The emerging strategy therefore appears to combine bargaining with endurance: seek an agreement while demonstrating that it can withstand the pressure without capitulating or abandoning its core terms.

This is why recent Iranian rhetoric deserves more attention than it has received.

Mohsen Rezaei, the new head of Iran’s supreme national security council, has called participation in Washington’s economic campaign an “act of war”. He says Tehran will first try to persuade neighbouring states not to participate, but has threatened their interests if they do. He has even warned that Iran could prevent Gulf oil exports through routes designed to bypass Hormuz.

These statements should not simply be dismissed as declarations of defiance for an audience in Iran. They reflect a consistent strategic logic: Iran cannot defeat the US economically, but it can try to make the economic strangulation of Iran prohibitively expensive for Washington and the countries it needs to enforce it.

That could mean tightening pressure on Hormuz, threatening infrastructure that enables alternative oil-export routes or putting greater pressure on US interests across the region. None of this would help ordinary Iranians. Escalation would compound their suffering. But that is precisely why Washington should think beyond the first-order effects of its own actions.

There is another weakness in Trump’s plan. For Bessent’s threat to work, Washington must persuade or coerce much of the world into participating, especially China, the principal buyer of Iranian oil. Yet Beijing is moving in the opposite direction. It has ordered firms not to comply with US sanctions targeting Chinese buyers of Iranian oil, while its top court recently highlighted a ruling penalising a Singaporean company for complying with US sanctions. Beijing has now warned it will take “all necessary measures” if Chinese interests are targeted.

Washington therefore faces an uncomfortable choice: tolerate continued trade between Iran and China, its neighbours and other partners, or dramatically escalate coercion of the governments, banks and companies that keep those channels open. That risks multiplying the US’s economic confrontations at a moment when it needs international cooperation to isolate Tehran. Bessent acknowledged the danger when asked why Washington was not immediately imposing its most sweeping secondary sanctions. “Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” he responded. That is quite an admission for an operation advertised as “economic D-day” .

With the midterms approaching, the White House has strong incentives to avoid another major escalation that could further disrupt Gulf energy flows and send fuel prices soaring. Tehran knows this. Its gamble is that it can endure and reroute enough commerce while imposing enough costs that Washington and its partners eventually prefer a settlement to continued confrontation.

That makes this a dangerous contest of endurance. Washington is betting Iran’s economy completely breaks first. Tehran is betting the US’s tolerance for the war and its mounting economic costs breaks first.

This has been the recurring flaw in Trump’s approach. In 2018, he left the 2015 nuclear deal with Iran, in an attempt to secure more favourable terms. Iran instead expanded its nuclear programme. Military conflict was supposed to force Tehran to accept US terms. Instead, the war expanded and Hormuz became a central source of Iranian leverage. Now intensified economic strangulation is supposed to accomplish what military power could not.

Unless Trump starts thinking several moves ahead, his latest attempt to force Iran into submission could leave the US with even higher energy prices, an even more confrontational adversary and yet another escalation it never counted on.

Sina Toossi is a senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, where his work focuses on US-Iran relations, US policy toward the Middle East and nuclear issues

editorials.title: A $1.95m deposit and $10k a month: welcome to the for-profit world of Australian aged care where no one is a winner
editorials.passage:
Y ou know you have entered the parallel universe of residential aged care when you find yourself saying, “Just to clarify, the deposit for the room is $1.95m, and the charges will be about $10,000 a month?”

“That’s correct,” the kindly sales agent replies.

Sure, it’s Sydney’s eastern suburbs, but that is a lot of money for a 20 sq metre room – almost double the median price for a one-bedroom apartment in the same suburb.

“In the brochure there are rooms for $1.25m – are they available?” you ask.

Sales agent: “No, and when the current residents leave [die], they will be renovated, with new bathrooms.”

“I guess that will make them more expensive?” you speculate.

Sales agent: “Yes, they will be $1.65m.”

Even with imported marble that seems excessive. Like all the privatised care services, the business of aged care is about property, cheap labour and public money.

But when your loved one has been deteriorating in a hospital bed for eight months without any therapies, eating hospital food on plastic plates, with only a car park to walk around, you are desperate and say yes, hoping against hope that another option will emerge.

In my case it did, and a few days later a 16 sq metre room with a big window in a well-run little centre became available. A mere $995,000 plus the day rate, the “hotelling fee”, non-clinical care contribution and special services charges .

Welcome to the for-profit, highly regulated, severely rationed, underpaid world of aged care – where no one is a winner, and the most frail and vulnerable and their carers are forced to navigate an extraordinarily complex system .

There are endless online forms to complete, passwords to remember, physical certification to prove you are who you say you are, then more documents to sign, financial advisers to consult, medical specialists to listen to, occupational therapists to perform for, providers to negotiate with and an ever-changing group of service providers and staff.

This time last year there were more than 2,000 older people in hospitals – “bed blockers” they were cruelly called – too frail to go home without more support, but with Buckley’s chance of finding a residential care bed, even if they could afford the now standard deposit of $750,000. Beds for the poorest and most needy were even scarcer .

This year, despite the state health ministers winning extra money from Canberra, the “bed blockers” are understood to have almost doubled.

The specialised facilities the frail elderly need cannot be conjured overnight. Last year few new beds became available nationwide. The health minister, Mark Butler, says a new facility is needed every 72 hours to meet the 18,000 target in three years .

The new aged care system, which was meant to address problems of the old model identified with heart-breaking detail by the royal commission into aged care, is not even a year old but already broken .

At least the Commonwealth Home Support Program, which costs 8% of the $40bn budget to assist 65% of aged care clients, will now continue until 2029.

Hundreds of thousands of people are waiting for assessments and, when these assessments are completed with an algorithm that doesn’t allow for human oversight, they find themselves waiting months for a package to meet their needs and enable them to age at home. When the package is allocated, they wait even longer for a provider to deliver the services they need.

For the three-quarters of aged people on pensions, the new co-payments for non-clinical services are often beyond their means.

That is, if they can find someone to do the work.

In the first two months of the new system, applications for financial hardship increased by 88%. “The way aged care reform is being implemented is causing harm … we have built inefficiency into the system by design,” the recently departed inspector general of aged care, Natalie Siegel-Brown, observed .

She believes the system should be turned upside down to start with the outcomes we want, rather than the mechanics of funding and services: to put care first, help people stay at home and connected to their communities.

This already occurs with the aged veterans’ care program .

It has also worked in countries including Denmark, Japan and South Korea, where investment in individual home care is prioritised, reducing the need for much more expensive residential facilities. It would mean a system where the assessor is a human being, where the person delivering meals warms them and sits down and talks with the client as they eat, where assistive technology is delivered when it is needed, not after months of checking and vetting and another fall.

All the ministerial platitudes in the world will not solve the problem. Action is needed, now, to keep people safely at home longer, before it becomes too hard, thousands of people and their carers needlessly suffer, and we all pay for it.

Julianne Schultz is the author of The Idea of Australia

editorials.title: Italy may ban staring at your phone while crossing the street. Why stop there?
editorials.passage:
I magine driving in Italy, with its narrow, cobblestone streets and scooter enthusiasts. I find it hard enough to drive in Los Angeles , a city designed specifically with the automobile in mind. I’d probably squash a pedestrian or two trying to navigate Italian roads.

The modern world is just too hectic for the ancient streets of Europe, so Italy is considering doing the only sensible thing it can: outlawing texting in crosswalks . The Italian government’s updated draft of its highway code proposes fines of €75 or more for anyone caught sending a DM, updating their LinkedIn, finishing Wordle on the fifth guess, or anything else phone-related that might make them miss an oncoming metal projectile. I’m sure most people will risk the slap on wrist to get that message off, but it at least sends a signal to the Italian people that paying attention to traffic is actually kind of important.

Distracted pedestrians aren’t just a problem in Italy , though. If I’m turning right on a red light, chances are there will be someone inching slowly toward the intersection with their thumbs furiously smashing against the glass of their iPhone, oblivious to the fact that I am planning to drive into the parcel of land they are currently occupying. It’s not just that this behavior is dangerous. It’s also deeply annoying . I’m forced to pay attention for both of us, like I’m a guardian angel or the arbiter of whether you, the clueless phone person, live or die. Sure, I might briefly get off on the power trip of having such authority over our mutual safety, but I’d much rather be thinking about where to have dinner instead of how long I should wait to honk at the drooling simpleton preventing me from turning.

I applaud the Italian government for their forward thinking. Actually, I think it’s time we criminalize more small annoyances. Such as …

Using a ringtone Someone please explain to me why anyone bothers with leaving their ringer on. We are decades past the era when, for a dollar, you could buy that Crazy Frog song and impress your friends every time you got a call. Now, it’s just pure sonic detritus, clogging up our ears with aural poison – bleeps, bloops, pings and plops. When AMC Theaters tells an auditorium full of grown adults to silence their phones before a movie, all I can think is: “Unless they’re an on-call heart surgeon, their phone should always be silent.” Fine amount: $200

Interrupting me when I’m not done talking I understand and accept that I have a lot to say. I make my meager living from writing, so pontificating just comes naturally to me. Sometimes, I wish it didn’t. But most of the time, what I’m saying is pretty important and you should be listening. Not waiting for your turn. I just listened to you try to captivate me with a treatise on gender roles in Christopher Nolan’s films. I respected you, even if I didn’t want to. Either let me finish or you’re fined! Fine amount: $200

Not pushing in your chair when stepping away from a table at a restaurant Would you like to see the server at your favorite Olive Garden location break their tibia because you left your chair in the middle of a walkway? If that’s what you think of our restaurant industry workers, I’ve got a mind to go outside to my patio and bang on some pots and pans like it’s Covid lockdown to thank everyone carrying a plate of shrimp scampi who has to avoid rude customers. When you get up from your table, push in your chair. It takes two seconds and it could save a life … and a plate of delicious pasta. Fine amount: $250

Riding an electric scooter on the sidewalk I would like to remind everyone that scooters from companies such as Lime and Lyft explicitly say to not ride these vehicles on the sidewalk. The sidewalk is called a sidewalk because it, much like Nancy Sinatra’s boots , was made for walking. A motorized conveyance doesn’t belong on the sidewalk, especially ones that actually can get some real speed behind them. Use the bike lane, for God’s sake. Or take the bus. Or anything else, really. It’s just beyond dangerous to be tooling around on a scooter while people are trying to go about their business.

I mean, what if I’m looking at my phone and texting? Shame on you, scooter guy. Fine amount: $500

Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humorist

editorials.title: A new sky: A pilgrimage in memory of my father – and his belief in the transformative power of tea
editorials.passage:
An old black cat slept snugly in its chair in the Yunnan-themed, street-facing restaurant on Mae Salong’s main road. It was oblivious to the gentle exhortations of two middle-aged women, who asked it to make way for three hungry travellers, excited about the halal fare served there. Beneath a picture of the Kaaba, photos of tantalising soups, noodles, and salads were hung.

The food was not quite Thai, not quite Burmese, certainly Yunnan-inspired, yet very familiar to the three of us. The neighbouring shop played Chinese pop music, and the signs around us were written in English, Thai and Chinese. On the street outside the restaurant, two bystanders spoke in accented Thai, telling us the cat was not going to move, so we ought to find another table.

We had driven two hours from Chiang Dao in northern Thailand in search of tea, supposedly the Assamica variety, grown in the region since the 1980s. My Thai-Australian friends had been here before and they remembered the road being rougher than the smooth, tarred highway we were on.

I, on the other hand, kept marvelling at the landscape, which reminded me of Northeast India. “We could be driving anywhere between Nagaland and upper Assam, you know,” I repeated.

My friends had sportingly gone along with my harebrained idea of seeking out Assam tea in unexpected places, a project that the Swedish anthropologist Bengt Karlsson is earnestly pursuing.

My purpose in pursuing the Assam tea bush was personal, as my father devoted his life to studying the plant and spreading it across Asia and Africa in the 20th century. His death on March 27, 2025, left me wishing I had learned more about his conviction that the tea bush could help address poverty in the global South.

Coming to Mae Salong felt like a secular pilgrimage in memory of a man who firmly believed that science and rationality should underpin civic life.

Tea is Mae Salong’s signature drink and local celebrity. It is often served free of charge in most restaurants and hotels as a welcome drink. “Number 17 is the one everyone likes, but you should try a newer one,” the auntie at the Yunnan restaurant insisted as we found a different table, away from the sleeping cat from the previous afternoon.

She poured us cups of amber liquid, its fragrance reaching our nostrils even before the cups were set in front of us. “We haven’t yet started packaging it,” she said, pointing to the big bag of oolong tea on the floor of her restaurant.

Our food arrived soon, and even the sight of Shan noodles and Yunnan beef with potatoes could not keep us from asking for more tea. It was the first of many cups we would be served across town. People would come alive whenever we showed interest in their array of tea packets.

My friend, the much-admired theatre personality Pongjit “Jon” Saphakhun, always slipped in a question about Assam tea during these encounters. This prompted further gestures of interest from our hosts, who confirmed they had once grown the Assam variety, but most of the tea they now sold was oolong, much sought after in Taiwan.

Between tea and Taiwan, Mae Salong was a repository of extraordinary stories that helped visitors make sense of the town’s tumultuous past. In fact, the town was emblematic of the layered history of conflict and cooperation that transformed a 20th-century frontier town with polyphonic identities into a Thai border town with historical, economic, and political ties to the outside world, ties that sit awkwardly with all forms of nationalism in Southeast Asia.

Mae Salong is also known by its official Thai name, Santikhiri. Situated in the highlands along the Burma/Myanmar-Thailand-Laos border, near China’s Yunnan province, the small town has a fascinating history of settlement. A polyglot place, it became home to various indigenous hill communities, such as the Akha, Hmong, and Lisu, as well as a sizeable number of Chinese communities from Yunnan.

The Yunnan Chinese belong to different religious groups, mainly Christian, Muslim, and Buddhist. In the 1950s, their ancestors established a small village in the highlands after the Chinese civil war, and they were all supporters of the nationalist Kuomintang. A section of the Kuomintang army refused to surrender to the Communists after the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949.

The 93rd Division, led by General Li Mi of the Kuomintang, continued to launch attacks against the Communists in Yunnan, but, given the vagaries of protracted warfare, it was left isolated from the main body of the nationalist army, which had moved to Taiwan along with General Chiang Kai-shek. The soldiers of the division first tried to negotiate a deal for refuge as political exiles with the newly independent Burmese government.

However, the Burmese government, wary of jeopardising its relationship with the Communist government in Beijing, attacked the Kuomintang division. Under these trying circumstances, the Chinese nationalists found themselves in the region that now constitutes the Myanmar-Thailand-Laos borderlands.

The region had been lightly administered by colonial Britain, as well as by Asian states such as Siam (renamed Thailand in 1939) and China. Following the Second World War and the Chinese Civil War, it became a refuge for a wide range of actors.

The indigenous communities that lived here were smaller and more egalitarian, with fewer ties to the global trade and cultural assimilation that characterised Asia in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Still, their homelands were carved up and shaped by larger historical forces, not always within their control.

The period between 1950 and 1970 was a pivotal era in the region. Decolonisation of Asian (and African) countries was underway as the Cold War expanded across the world. British, Dutch, French, Portuguese, and Spanish powers were withdrawing from their colonies, leaving behind lands where several ethnic groups vied with their neighbours for control. They adopted various ideologies and strategies to establish their control over the territories they sought to govern.

When the Kuomintang soldiers were pushed out of Myanmar, they moved to the area around Mae Salong. There, they attempted to regroup and re-establish contact with the main force that had consolidated its base in Taiwan. From the 1960s to the early 1980s, the Thai government faced a Communist-inspired insurgency that the Thai military, with help from the Central Intelligence Agency, brutally crushed.

Members of the 93rd Division were enlisted in the north because they had a long history of fighting Communist guerrillas during the Chinese Civil War. In return, the Chinese soldiers and their families were granted Thai citizenship.

Elements of Thai and Chinese nationalism coexist in Mae Salong. Buddhist temples dot the hilltops, while an elegant, spare mosque sits midway up a hill overlooking the town. References to the Kuomintang are impossible to miss, with the walls of restaurants and homes adorned with elaborate murals and artworks celebrating the movement’s figures. General Chiang Kai-shek figures prominently among them, as do ordinary soldiers and supporters.

Along the lower part of town, the highway leads to an elaborate memorial to the fallen Kuomintang soldiers, where the Thai and Taiwanese flags are displayed in the main spirit hall. The memorial proudly commemorates the wars – both victories and defeats – fought by the 93rd Division.

Rooms in the complex are dedicated to different aspects of the Chinese soldiers’ political journey and record the contributions of the Taiwan government, as well as those of a host of other entities that helped establish small-scale business enterprises in Mae Salong.

Roosters begin crowing early in the morning in Mae Salong. Like the cats, they are everywhere and are treated with good humour by those around them. Both cats and roosters keep to their lane and are unlikely to be seen darting across streets or running through people’s homes.

I woke to a particularly raucous specimen who decided to announce the arrival of sunrise around 4.30 in the morning. The sun had just begun to bathe the valley outside my window in light. Beyond the rooster’s loud cries stretched vast acres of tea, neatly planted in rows. From my table on the balcony, I watched the tea bushes, separated from the bamboo thickets, as I waited for my tea and toast, the earliest breakfast I had had in a while.

The waiter smiled and said something in Burmese, and seeing my confusion, shook his head and said something to the two women with thanaka paste on their cheeks. All three began to apologise and giggle at once. The early-morning tea was exquisite. The town had several small kiosks, tea rooms, and tea-processing factories overlooking the spectacular hill slopes, each serving hot and iced teas, along with the ubiquitous premium coffee for which Thailand is becoming famous. The hills that ringed the town were dotted with quirky establishments, including one with four fountains pouring water through teapots.

July was a lean tourist season, so most waiters and servers at these establishments were happy to chat with inquisitive visitors about the town's fortunes and tea. The moment Jon mentioned my interest in Assam tea, or that I was trying to follow in my father’s footsteps, our hosts would pull out photographs and point to packets labelled “Forest Tea” to show that the Assamica variety of Camellia sinensis was still around.

It had been brought to the area in the 1980s, around the time the Kuomintang veterans and their families were granted Thai citizenship. In 2009, sociologist Ko-lin Chin wrote that the Kuomintang had begun partnering with ethnic warlords in northern Myanmar. As a result, it is alleged that some Chinese soldiers and ethnic warlords encouraged indigenous farmers to cultivate opium, which they taxed and transported across the region known as the Golden Triangle.

My father strongly believed that the tea plant grown in Assam could help alleviate poverty in the global South. As he aged, he would wait patiently for me to finish my rant about the terrible working conditions on the tea plantations, then softly add that the plant itself was a thing of beauty and wonder.

I could almost sense his joy at being invited by the government to northern Thailand, and that too, for as noble an enterprise as replacing opium with tea. He spent a short time in the region, arranging the transfer of tea clones and technology, but the Assamica variety did not become the star he had hoped it would be.

In the 1990s, Assam tea was replaced by oolong varieties from mainland China. This coincided with the renewal of ties between Taiwan and the Chinese community in Mae Salong.

One of the main rooms in the memorial dedicated to martyrs contained a detailed record of the contributions of the Chinese Association for Relief and Ensuing Services and the Free China Relief Association. It noted that CARES and FCRA had helped re-establish connections between the community and their comrades in Taiwan, including support for livelihood options. Growing tea and livestock and providing scholarships for young people to study in Taiwan were integral to this effort.

“There are many young people who get scholarships and leave for Taiwan,” said Achin, a community historian and tea taster, whom we met at Plantation 101, where she worked. She pointed out the teas we were going to drink and went about the ceremonial work with practised ease. Her grandfather was a veteran, and she said she had been working at the tea-tasting counter for several years.

Few of the youth came back, she said. Taiwan offered them better work and opportunities, so they did not want to return to a life of ennui in the mountains of northern Thailand. “I often felt like we were left behind when I was younger,” she said to Jon, but explained that she felt more aligned with her Chinese heritage and Thai citizenship these days.

Achin spoke about the difficulties faced by the early Chinese community as they settled on the hill slopes around Mae Salong. Ordinary Thai people from the lowlands were afraid to travel up, and the Chinese feared what might happen if they engaged with the lowland communities, having had a bad experience in northern Burma.

The indigenous people of the region, wedged between the lowland Thai and the armed Chinese soldiers, chose to side with the latter. However, significant numbers of them supported the Communist Party of Thailand’s armed insurgents.

Assam tea, therefore, was the result of a series of complex calculations and negotiations among the various actors, except perhaps the Communist Party of Thailand. Even today, Achin explained, indigenous Akha and Hmong villagers continued to grow the Assamica variety in their fields. Many of these teas were left unpruned and marketed as “Forest Black Tea” across town.

These teas were bolder in flavour, less delicate than the oolongs usually offered to visitors at tea-tasting sessions. However, they were not marketed as green teas. “Green tea is lazy tea,” Achin said, chuckling, as she poured us another glass of delicate oolong from one of the larger factories in town. Jon concurred, recounting her earliest memories of drinking stronger teas branded “Three Horses Tea” across Thailand.

Our conversations with Achin were in fluent Thai, though she reminded us that she spoke Chinese at home. “The moment we step out, we are Thai,” she said with a smile.

She spoke about the difficulties the Taiwan connection posed for young students in Mae Salong. Her generation and those growing up now had to learn Thai in government and private schools during the day, as the Thai state sought to establish cultural control over the place and its people. By evening, the Taiwanese government’s financial aid required students to learn Chinese as well, so they had to attend extra classes at night.

This explained a puzzle for my friends and me. We were confused by the sight of schoolchildren waiting for their parents to pick them up at 7pm outside the Baptist School the previous evening. They were learning Chinese so that their passage to Taiwan might be a little easier if they chose to apply for a scholarship to leave Mae Salong.

The news of devastating landslides in Mon district, Nagaland, and once-in-a-lifetime floods in upper Assam reached me as I wrote the concluding paragraphs of this travel diary. Videos of panicked people, livestock, and wildlife, desperate for help amid the raging brown waters cascading down the mountains, reminded me of the fragility of the places we call home.

Short videos, shared thousands of times, showed entire mountains cave in to become mudslides; frightened pythons drowning in floodwaters and struggling to enter through windows, behind which terrified people waited for both water and snake to enter; and people perched on treetops as the sea of water raced towards an already swollen Brahmaputra and its tributaries.

I read my friend, geologist Sarat Phukan’s evocative piece , in which he described the flood’s aftermath as “a new sky over an old, bruised valley”. He painstakingly explained that illegal mining, earth cutting, and the construction of four-laned highways contributed to the flood. Even though it is still early, news from back home confirmed that many of my friends and family have lost their livelihoods, homes, and livestock and may not recover from this devastation in their lifetime.

It reminded me of conversations with my friends, Jon and Richard, as we sat and ate lunch by the Kok River in Thaton on our way down from Mae Salong. I was intrigued by the intensive cultivation of the hillsides, both at Mae Salong and on the way back to Chiang Dao. What looked like pristine forests were a patchwork of agricultural enterprise. Large conglomerates had persuaded farmers to grow crops for the market, and every inch of hillside had been planted.

This growth required more houses, so local riverbeds were mined for sand and pebbles. More dams on the Mekong to supply electricity for industries in Thailand had also compounded the problem. Jon and the waitress talked about the 2024 flooding of the Kok River. The waitress pointed to a building on the opposite side and said the water had risen to the second floor. Her own restaurant had been swept away, and we were sitting in the new section. Ironically, the song playing as we ate was about the romance associated with the Kok River.

Our fates in Northeast India and northern Thailand are not so different after all. The states that govern us see our territories as fallow land, devoid of enterprising people, associations, and conglomerations that can add economic value. Each new group that comes to seek shelter from political storms is encouraged to do more to prove it belongs to the land. The authorities exact a heavy price from the land and its people.

When disasters occur, as they did in northern Thailand (and Laos) in 2024 and in eastern Assam, Nagaland and Arunachal Pradesh this year, the authorities are often slower to respond than our neighbours and communities that rally around namghors, mosques, churches, temples, and secular institutions such as schools and colleges.

I think my father was among those who went to persuade, but not for a profiteer’s motive. In the last years of his life, he had long conversations with my partner about changes in the weather and their implications for our region. She remembers how accurately he would predict rain after a spell of humid summer days.

During my brief time in northern Thailand, I tried to see the land through his eyes. He was an agronomist, but he was also curious about people and their histories. Would he have felt bad that his beloved Assam tea had given way to more delicate and marketable oolongs from China? I think not; he would have found his way to the Akha village below our hotel to advise the growers on the right balance of sun and shade for a prolonged harvest.

Maybe I should have asked him more about his work when I was younger, but then I would not have made this pilgrimage to Mae Salong. Some tragedies happen in an instant, yet they build up slowly. Identities and landscapes usually take generations to take shape, shaped by different forms of pressure at various moments. Plants, people, and politics go on to make places what they are. A few days in Mae Salong is hardly enough to make sense of the momentous changes the borderland town has witnessed over seven decades.

However, pilgrimages allow us to hope for better futures, even after we return home. As we wrestled with state politics and people’s memories and made our way down from the town’s only mosque, Jon pointed excitedly to a rainbow above us. “Look, in memory of your father! There is hope, darling,” she said with childlike glee.

Sanjay Barbora teaches sociology at the University of California, Santa Cruz.

editorials.title: ‘Covid should have brought the working class and upper class together. It did not’: Jyoti Yadav
editorials.passage:
A Covid book in 2026? Why now, one might ask, when that catastrophic chapter has been so thoroughly buried, so deliberately archived into a past we’ve collectively agreed not to revisit? But that question answers itself. The forgetting is precisely the point.

When the state collapsed in 2020-21, it abandoned, even actively endangered, the people it claimed to protect – there was no reckoning. No accountability, no honest audit of what elected representatives chose not to do while pyres burned in public parks and oxygen ran out in hospitals.

Jyoti Yadav’s book, Faith and Fury: Covid Dispatches from India’s Hinterlands, refuses that erasure. It is at once journalism and defiance – to remember what was done, what was not done, and who suffered for both. In today’s media landscape, ground reporting has been hollowed out, intimidated, and economically starved. Yet Yadav’s book is also a testament to what journalism can still be when someone travels through a world shut down, to find stories that are preferred to be hidden away.

In a conversation with Scroll , Yadav spoke about the making of the book, the crisis of memory surrounding the pandemic years, her experience with social media, and what it means to practice journalism now. Excerpts from the interview:

How did the title come to be? The title was given by Rama Lakshmi, my features editor at The Print . We were clear from the start: no burning fires on the cover, no Covid or hellish words in the title. Covid could appear in the subtitle, but not the title itself. We also wanted to avoid a harrowing image of crematoriums.

If you read the stories, people were furious, but there was also faith; citizens came forward to help fellow citizens. So we decided to go with Faith and Fury.

For many urban middle-class Indians, Covid has a nostalgic tint – lockdown boredom, isolation, the loss of ordinary pleasures. For much of India, though, as your book shows, it was highways, crematoria, oxygen shortages, ASHA workers, and rural hospitals. How do you see this split in national memory, and is that also part of what shapes our mainstream discourse around Covid? If the working class protests poor management at a district hospital in Gurugram after someone dies of negligence, the upper class says it is happening elsewhere. We have nothing to do with it, because we do not use district hospitals. The government system is meant for the poor. That is the worldview of a tiny but influential population: healthcare gaps, ASHA workers, and public hospitals are someone else’s problem.

But Covid also neutralised things. Someone living in DLF Camellias in Gurugram could go to Fortis, but even Fortis had no beds. I saw people seeking beds in government hospitals because private ones had locked their doors. All forms of transportation were restricted for everybody.

Covid should have brought both classes together.
