The influential class should have developed a more empathetic view of the working class – their wages, their suffering – and advocated for better policies. Even a former chief minister was waiting in a queue for hospitalisation. We all deserve better hospitals, better facilities, and an accountable government. But it didn’t happen. Once cases decreased by June or July, the split remained. Migrants most affected in the first wave are poorer than before; in Noida, they are asking for Rs 23 a day and being beaten by the police. The same treatment. The gap is not being bridged. It is widening.

Was there a difference in writing this book compared to writing long-form articles? Was there a challenge, or something new you discovered? In journalism, you file a story and see it on the website the very next day; that acts as fuel. You get the thrill of being a reporter: people talk about it, there is some impact, and you move to the next story. Writing a book was a very different – boring, dull, and lonely – process. With Covid, every chapter deals with death. Eventually, I decided to put it plainly: death is death. I won’t exaggerate the pain and suffering. Once I stopped struggling to make this a masterpiece and focused on documenting the story, it became easier, because the difficult part – the reporting – was already done.

Reporting was harder than writing. You could have become a statistic yourself. I don’t know how I escaped the virus so many times. There was also exhaustion: two months on the road, one day stretching into the next.

At the heart of this book, and much of your journalism, are stories. We now live in a media climate where journalism is often reduced to facts and neutral descriptions, and narratives, emotions, or any moral clarity is quickly dismissed as bias. What role do stories play for you as a journalist? Every now and then, someone would crib about how Indian journalism is dead. There is a discomfort among upper-caste and upper-class journalists in India – earlier it was their fold – and I see my entry in that light. There is a study showing that 90% of leadership roles in legacy newsrooms come from one set: same food habits, same world exposure, same convent schools, same universities. They all become journalists, and they have a single lens through which to view India.

If you see a woman working in the fields in rural India, as an outsider, you’ll feel she’s suppressed, that she doesn’t have a voice. But she might own that land, and that work might empower her. I come from the second group. I have an insider’s view.

If you do not have Scheduled Caste, Tribal, Haryanvi, or Rajasthani representation in a newsroom, and someone who grew up in Bombay is writing about Haryana and Rajasthan, then prejudices and stereotypes reflect in the headlines. I’m from Haryana. I’m not going to romanticise my vision, but I’m also not going to report the way my editor thinks I should report on female foeticide. My stories were fresh even for my editors, and they started trusting my lens and my instinct.

In I Am on the Hit List , Rollo Romig writes that when we think of Indian journalism, we think of big newsrooms like The Times of India and Hindustan Times . But the greatest threat to state power often comes from independent journalists, who remain invisible to mainstream conversation. Journalism is not dead; look at the stories being filed by vernacular journalists. Look at award nominations, and you’ll find 300 good stories. Good journalism is happening. It’s just not going viral on social media. Old-fashioned, long-form text journalism is alive. There is, however, very little being done to sustain it.

When you’re doing ground reportage while the larger narrative is being shaped elsewhere, does that create a sense of pessimism? I don’t get affected by that noise. The star anchors are all podcasters – driving money, driving impact, getting more visibility. But I’m only a decade into journalism, and I strongly believe that when the noise is over, good journalism will shine.

I have seen this with the Bhanwari Devi story from Rajasthan, over 6,000 words. A digital portal would normally say this was not their story. Yet we went ahead. Features usually draw low readership; they remain at the bottom. But the Bhanwari Devi story stayed at the top of our website for at least two days, and for a year or two after, it kept being shared by people who had never followed The Print or my work. People read it till the last word.

A podcast cannot compete with powerful long-form text that brings real change, whether through litigation or rehabilitation. But for that, we need to be active on social media. In 21st-century India, reporting is not enough; you need readership and influence. Prime-time anchors may have more resources than we do, but we are not helpless. The medium is decentralised and democratic. We need to find creative ways to engage with a story.

Similarly, it’s not important to just write books; you also need to talk about them. I was born into digital journalism during the rise of The Wire, Newslaundry , and The Print in 2016. I know how keywords work and the role X plays in making a story viral. You need to create impact and stay engaged with your audience. The real work begins after the book is published.

Social media trolling appears prominently across the first few chapters – whenever you discuss a piece, there’s this undercurrent of anxiety about how it will be received online. Journalism in India is already difficult, but for women journalists, that hostility becomes more personal, more sexualised, more relentless. What role does social media play in your journalism – not just as a reporting or amplification tool, but also as a site of harassment and even violence? Since the reporting in the book was during 2020 and 2021, I used to tweet a lot – about India’s political discourse, mostly critical of the ruling party, which has the most powerful IT Cell. My tweets would be screenshotted, and if I had reported on some urgent issue, that screenshot would soon translate into online sexual violence.

The initial trolling made me start self-censoring. Before my stories were published, I had nightmares about the headlines my editors might give, and how I would be trolled for words that weren’t even mine. The most problematic part was the sexualisation. The second was the casteist undertone; carrying a Yadav surname, I would be seen as representative of a politically influential caste group. I was never someone who took pride in or defended my gender, caste, or state identity. But I became more conscious of it because of the trolling. I stopped pitching stories that might upset certain sections on X, which is very dangerous. I could have left journalism.

But I navigated that space. I started posting less on X. I knew I was here for a long innings. I cannot create an environment where this leads to physical violence. We have seen this with Ravish Kumar; he cannot go on the ground and report by himself anymore. Seeing what happened with Rana Ayyub, Arfa Khanum, Neha Dixit, I got very calculative about what I post. So I stopped tweeting about political discourse entirely.

The sexualised trolling affects your personal relationships – your marital life, your relationship with your parents – because they get to see everything. And during the Covid coverage, I thought: if I test positive, what if they hang me for spreading the coronavirus?

Has the self-censoring stopped now? No, it’s a work in progress. The algorithm and leadership have changed, and it’s more toxic. But my self-censorship is limited to X, not journalism. If I think a story is important and urgent, I do it.

Covid is arguably one of the most documented crises of our time – photos, videos, dashboards, hospital footage – and yet we have largely forgotten it, particularly the failures of the state. How does that paradox exist? After the 1975 Emergency, people came together to remove Congress despite its giant status. And yet, that collective reckoning never happened with Covid. I do not have concrete answers. What I observed on my return visits to the same towns and meeting the same people was that the anger was gone within a year. Maybe people wanted to leave the tragedy behind, didn’t want to revisit those memories. I don’t know whether it was collective or forced forgetting, whether the state had a role to play. Only if you do have time do you get bored and think about all the horrifying things that happened, whether the state succeeded or failed. Perhaps we are always scrolling; there is no space to reflect, so people move on.

I interviewed a migrant back in his village, someone who had every reason to be angry at the state for not protecting his rights, for not giving him any safety net. He was asked to leave because his employer couldn’t pay him, taking a four-day journey standing without food or water, reaching home… and he was not angry. They’ll say “system,” but there is no face to that word. Maybe they have become so used to it.

Covid was not an isolated experience for a few thousand people; it was a once-in-a-lifetime experience for everyone. If someone did not lose a family member, they likely lost a job, except for the elite class with all the facilities. What your caste was, what your location was, what your identity was; you suffered accordingly.

But it is now a tale. This migrant tells me: “Around that time, I left Bombay. I walked for a night and a day, then we found a truck. My mother took a loan of Rs 5,000 and sent it to me on GPay. We paid Rs 4,000 to the truck driver. We were dropped off at Darbhanga, and then we walked another night.” Yet he is not angry. He brings out the basket given by the state when he was quarantined in a government school – dilapidated infrastructure, no fans, no electricity, packed together in a room during the April-May heatwave. They still have the PPE kits they were given and use them as a roof covering. That is what I generally discover in the homes of those who suffered the most.

It was crucial to document it because, once we are 10 years away from Covid, who will believe it? People have very individual experiences; one family has the oxygen experience, another the lack of hospital testing experience. It was important to put these stories together, and fortunately, I had captured them chronologically, in their entirety, from the beginning.

During the book launch, MP Manoj Jha coined the term “forced forgetting.” It is not something people did on their own. It was forced by the state, by the machinery. Perhaps someone else will fully analyse why people moved on.

You have been working for about a decade in journalism – a very tumultuous time for journalists across the spectrum. How do you view journalism in India today, and what shifts have you experienced? I’m very optimistic. Difficult times produce difficult journalism. I’ve seen young women journalists at The Print who are feisty, who report fiercely across issues.

The only worry is sustainability. A podcaster will make more money, but there are not enough grants to support long-form journalism. Ground reporting cannot happen without someone paying for it; it demands money. If I report on bonded labourers in Bihar for a month, and someone makes a reel on it without even crediting my story while getting more eyeballs, that is disheartening. But it doesn’t discourage me, because I love journalism and ground reporting.

People talk about AI replacing journalism, but that’s not the case. AI can summarise my story, but it cannot tell you what it felt like to speak to a woman rescued from bonded labour, hear about three decades of unpaid work, and look at her fingers and tell the story. Journalism today is about context. Breaking stories is no longer enough. Fifty people were killed. But why? Who were they? That is for the journalist to find out.

One government action and newsrooms run away – professors put in jail, women’s commissions weaponised. If it’s happening to a professor, it can happen to anyone. If you only enjoy state impunity when you are on good terms with them, you stop questioning. We just need good editors, good promoters, and good readers. That’s enough.

What are you reading currently, and do you have a next in mind? I just finished Neha Dixit’s The Many Lives of Syeda X . The writing is beautiful, but what blew my mind is the work behind it: the number of interviews, the corroboration. I’m also reading Rohini Mohan’s The Seasons of Trouble: Life Amid the Ruins of Sri Lanka’s Civil War .

The next book is with Westland. I wanted to look at the last ten years of India through the lives of rural women. Eight women, eight chapters, eight characters. It is about India through the lives of women.

editorials.title: At New York event, Bhagwat preaches ‘oneness in diversity’ amid a storm of protests
editorials.passage:
On the morning of August 29, more than 5,000 people of Indian-origin trickled into New York’s Madison Square Garden to see one man take the stage: Mohan Bhagwat, the chief of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, the ideological parent of India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.

The event was titled the “Universal Oneness Celebration”. But outside the arena, there were two starkly different worlds.

On one side of the entrance sidewalk, attendees in festive clothes, saffron caps and rakhis took photographs in front of the Madison Square Garden logo. In one corner, a man played the dhol and sang a rap-like version of Jana Gana Mana. “Being woke is a joke,” he shouted. “We love Modi ji,” he continued, referring to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, as some others joined in to shout “Vande Mataram”.

On the other side stood coalitions protesting Bhagwat’s appearance on grounds that the RSS and BJP fostered a climate of hate and violence against religious minorities in India. On Wednesday, echoing the same concerns, the US Commission on International Religious Freedom had urged the Trump administration to revoke Bhagwat’s visa.

But the demonstrations on Saturday, organised by groups including Hindus for Human Rights and the Indian American Muslim Council , seldom bothered the attendees, many of whom had travelled from far and beyond to see Bhagwat speak.

“I saw Modi when he was here. It was wow. It was a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity and I got it,” said Neelima Kallaru, who posed in front of the stadium with her husband and friends, referring to Modi’s public address in Long Island in September 2024. “And now I got the second one. There was no way I would miss it,” she said.

Her husband, Murali Kallaru, who immigrated from Andhra Pradesh to the US in 2000, felt similarly. The cacophony of protest slogans did not bother him either, he said.

“This is about India, not just about Hindutva,” said Kallaru. “It’s one family. And families can have different opinions,” he continued, referring to the demonstrations that had grown in numbers as the event got closer.

As the crowds began entering the arena, chants echoed: from “Vande Mataram” to “Jai Shri Ram”. The attendees were ushered in by volunteers with the Hindu Swayamsevak Sangh, the RSS’s offshoot in the United States. The hall was packed to the brim.

The event, ostensibly centred on celebrating “Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam” or “the world is one family”, began with a call to action from the organisers, the American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue . The world is one, they said, calling around 48 faith leaders to the stage.

Then entered the guest of honour, Bhagwat. He was welcomed with a standing ovation.

He sat next to three people: a rabbi, an imam and a reverend. Each of them spoke one after the other. The common theme was “oneness”.

“It is one world, one humanity,” said Talib M Shareef, president and imam of Washington DC’s Masjid Muhammad and a retired US Air Force member. “Not one religion. Not one culture. Not one language. Not one ethnicity. Not one nationality. But one humanity.”

Finally, at the end of the nearly three-hour-long event, the RSS chief spoke.

For nearly 45 minutes, Bhagwat expounded on the “unity of existence” and “dharma”, which he said stood for balance, not religion.

“I come from a country where there is oneness in diversity,” he said. “We celebrate it.”

The RSS chief claimed a Hindu who does not want Muslims to live in India cannot be considered a Hindu. “If you want to call yourself Hindu, you must believe that all paths lead to the same goal and that every human has dignity,” he said.

Bhagwat told the Indians in the 5,000-odd crowd sitting in front of him to “be loyal” to their “karmabhoomi” or place of work – the United States. Their “janmabhoomi” or place of birth, India, “expects [them] to live the value imparted” to them.

“And the value is oneness,” he said. The crowd burst into cheers.

Bhagwat’s speech was, in many ways, starkly different from his last major public speech in the US, according to Ajit Sahi, the Director of Public Affairs of the Indian American Muslim Council.

In 2018, at the World Hindu Congress in Chicago, Bhagwat spoke about the need for Hindus to “come together”, comparing them to a lion that could be overwhelmed by wild dogs if it stood alone.

“You have to remember that [speech],” said Sahi, who was one of the primary organisers of the protests outside Madison Square Garden on Saturday morning. “And now he is speaking about oneness?” he continued.

The contrast had become a central theme of the opposition to Bhagwat’s visit in the days leading up to his appearance.

On Tuesday, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he opposed the event, describing the RSS’s vision as “exclusionary” and at odds with the pluralistic and secular India he said he had grown up knowing. Mamdani, however, said the city might not have jurisdiction to cancel a private event at Madison Square Garden.

The same day, former New York city comptroller Brad Lander and city council members Shahana Hanif, Lincoln Restler and Julie Won joined more than 40 civil rights and community organisations at City Hall to call on Madison Square Garden to cancel the event.

Lander invoked the arena’s history as the site of a 1939 rally by the German American Bund. “MSG said it would not host hate-filled, bigoted rallies again,” he said. “It should not host this one.”

Hanif said Madison Square Garden should not provide a platform to Bhagwat and the RSS, which she described as a movement with a “documented history of persecution and violence against religious minorities”.

By Wednesday, the opposition had moved beyond New York.

The US Commission on International Religious Freedom called on the Trump administration to consider targeted sanctions against RSS members and Indian officials involved in religious-freedom violations, and specifically urged the government to revoke Bhagwat’s US visa.

“The US government has an opportunity to hold India accountable and signal that the United States stands for religious freedom for the people of India,” said the commission’s vice chair, CeCe Heil. Not doing so would only lead to more attacks on minorities by “vigilante mobs,” she added.

The commission’s recommendation was non-binding, and Bhagwat remained in the country.

On Thursday, 65 US organisations, including Hindu, Muslim, Sikh, Christian, Jewish, Dalit and civil-rights groups, issued a joint statement denouncing Bhagwat’s visit.

As the controversy intensified, on Friday evening, Bhagwat’s face appeared on one of the giant digital billboards in Times Square. The images were accompanied by the words “Resolve, Harmony, Dialogue”, an unmistakable display of the public-relations campaign surrounding his visit.

The event itself was organised by AHEAD, a little-known nonprofit established in 2025. AHEAD presents itself as an organisation dedicated to engagement and dialogue among American Hindus and other communities.

But two recent investigations by Savera , a US-based organisation that researches Hindu nationalist networks, have questioned how independent AHEAD is from the RSS’s American infrastructure.

Savera reported that AHEAD was incorporated in May 2025, with its initial registration connected to Khanderao Kand, a longtime RSS and HSS figure and founder of the Foundation for India and Indian Diaspora Studies.

The report found that the organisation’s three listed directors also had connections to the American Sangh: Sudesh Agrawal, one of the directors, heads the HSS’s Cleveland chapter, while other directors have participated in HSS or affiliated organisations.

Savera also reported that AHEAD’s name and the “Universal Oneness” branding echoed language used by HSS in its own programming. It characterised AHEAD as part of a broader network through which the RSS’s overseas operations could organise Bhagwat’s visit while maintaining a separate formal identity. AHEAD has not publicly described itself as an RSS or HSS organisation.

By Saturday morning, the argument over Bhagwat’s visit had, hence, become larger than the event itself.

Inside Madison Square Garden, thousands of people listened to him. Neither did Bhagwat mention the opposition to his visit, nor anything about India or Prime Minister Modi.

Outside, protesters argued that giving the RSS chief one of New York’s most prominent stages was itself a statement about who gets to define that “oneness” – and its history.

All photographs by Oishika Neogi.

editorials.title: Behind Xi’s swagger lies urgency: Why Delhi must bargain hard with Beijing
editorials.passage:
Zhou Enlai was a fascinating personality. A sharp and sophisticated diplomat-politician, he played a crucial role in creating — and selling — Mao Zedong’s more benign image to the world. If Edgar Snow was the American Trojan horse who helped portray China’s communists as “farmers” and “rebels” who, with Western support, might eventually become “democrats”, Zhou was the Middle Kingdom’s desi boy: urbane, reassuring and instrumental in humanising Communist China and normalising Mao abroad.

Yet, even such unflinching loyalty could not ultimately protect Zhou from Mao’s cruelty. As Zhou battled cancer in his final years, Mao reportedly restricted aspects of his medical treatment, adding to the suffering of a man who had served him faithfully for decades.

But Zhou is not the principal protagonist here. He matters because his story illustrates something fundamental about China: the gulf between perception and reality. Let’s look at Xi Jinping, for instance. The Chinese President is widely seen as tough and obstinate, a leader who rarely bends and expects others to accommodate him. But is he really so inflexible? The answer offers clues about how Bharat should deal with China.

When Xi emerged as China’s paramount leader, he was a largely unknown personality. A popular joke went: “Who’s Xi Jinping? Ah, he’s Peng Liyuan’s husband.” One veteran Japanese journalist even published a book in early 2012 titled Xi Jinping: Communist China’s Weakest Emperor. Many who thought they knew Xi would soon discover how badly they had misread him. Nicholas Kristof, the former China correspondent and Pulitzer Prize winner, was optimistic enough to proclaim in The New York Times in January 2013 that “change is coming” to China under Xi. He predicted that “Mao’s body will be hauled out of Tiananmen Square on his watch, and Liu Xiaobo, the Nobel Peace Prize-winning writer, will be released from prison”.

There were reasons for such expectations. Before reaching the pinnacle of power, Xi made remarkably few enemies and kept his cards close to his chest. As Chun Han Wong writes in Party of One, local officials and journalists saw him as “a cautious and somewhat nondescript administrator”. Wong also quotes Alfred Wu, a politics professor who encountered Xi while working as a newspaper reporter in Fuzhou: “Back then he was rather bland and passive — even if he had the authority to do something, he often didn’t use it.”

There is a lesson here about the political culture of China’s Communist Party, with its peculiar Confucian inheritance: what is visible may reveal remarkably little about what lies underneath. Chinese leaders have long been adept at showing the outside world what they want it to see. From Deng Xiaoping until Xi Jinping’s arrival, China projected the reassuring idea of a “peaceful rise”. Deng’s dictum was to hide China’s strength and bide its time. Once Beijing concluded that it possessed the economic, military and diplomatic power to assert itself more openly, much of that restraint disappeared.

Xi has become both the symbol and instrument of that transformation. The contrast with his predecessor has been striking. “Hu (Jintao, who was Xi Jinping's immediate predecessor) could walk into a room with his staffers and you wouldn’t know he was the leader, other than the fact that he’s standing in front,” Ben Rhodes, a former deputy national security adviser to Barack Obama, once recalled. “Xi has swagger, the confidence of being the boss.”

However, behind that swagger lies urgency. Beijing appears to be in a hurry to become the world’s pre-eminent power. It has accelerated the modernisation of the People’s Liberation Army. And because power is exercised through narratives as much as missiles and money, it has dramatically expanded its diplomatic machinery. By 2019, as Wong writes in Party of One, “Xi had nearly doubled Beijing’s diplomatic spending to some 62 billion yuan, or roughly $9 billion, and turned the Chinese foreign ministry into the world's largest diplomatic network, with some 276 embassies, consulates, and other missions globally, surpassing that of the US State Department.”

This brings us to the question that also has immense significance for Bharat: Why is China in such a hurry?

One answer is that time may no longer be entirely on Beijing’s side. China is slowing down, and some of the forces behind that slowdown are structural rather than cyclical. Beijing must increasingly contemplate the possibility that the extraordinary growth rates that powered its stupendous rise for four decades will not return.

More troubling still is demography. China is confronting the consequences of decades of coercive population control: a shrinking workforce, an ageing population and a worsening dependency ratio. China was extraordinarily efficient at adopting Western technology, management practices and economic ideas. It was equally efficient at embracing some of the worst Western assumptions about population and development. Bharat pursued population control too, but its characteristically slower and less efficient state machinery — so often blamed for holding the country back — may have prevented it from travelling as far down the same demographic road.

China now confronts the prospect of growing old before it becomes truly rich. That creates urgency, especially among mandarins.

For Bharat, this presents both challenges and opportunities. Beijing initially appeared to believe it could pressure Delhi using an older playbook. But Bharat has changed in recent years. Doklam and Galwan demonstrated both the risks Beijing was prepared to take and the limits of coercion against its south-western neighbour.

China must also contend with a much larger strategic challenge: the United States. Xi’s China increasingly views the international system through a G2 prism. America is its principal strategic competitor, and Beijing appears to regard the top position in the global hierarchy as attainable if it plays its cards well. The disruption of America’s traditional alliances and partnerships under Donald Trump has reinforced Beijing’s sense that an opportunity exists.

Xi, therefore, has reasons to seek an accommodation with Bharat. This is not because Beijing suddenly believes the two countries can become friends. Great powers do not need to trust each other to find cooperation useful. China’s relationship with Russia is a case in point: beneath public declarations of a “no limits” partnership lie historical distrust and strategic anxiety, as a recent diplomatic cable suggests. Yet, Moscow and Beijing cooperate because their interests overlap.

Xi may want something similar — though necessarily more limited — with Bharat. China is unlikely to stop supporting Pakistan. Nor will Beijing abandon its growing engagement with Bangladesh and the wider Indian neighbourhood. Instead, it can combine pressure with accommodation — the geopolitical equivalent of good cop, bad cop. As former diplomat Vijay Gokhale argues in China’s Wars, Bharat should prepare for prolonged Chinese “grey-zone” coercion. Beijing’s objectives remain broadly twofold: prevent Bharat from becoming firmly embedded in an American-led balancing coalition against China, and constrain Delhi’s ability to challenge Beijing’s preferred regional order.

This is what makes the current moment important. As speculation grows about Xi Jinping coming to Delhi with a massive delegation reportedly numbering more than 400 people, Bharat should recognise that beneath the bluster, Beijing may have reasons to compromise. China, after all, faces slower growth, demographic decline, intensifying technological competition and a more difficult external environment. The waiting game that served Deng’s China so brilliantly may no longer suit Xi’s China.

This means Beijing may be willing to improve ties, even if tactically. Delhi, too, should pursue normalisation with Beijing. Their ties cannot be permanently hostage to the history of distrust between the two nations. At the same time, maturity does not require historical amnesia.

If Xi Jinping comes to Delhi next month, as expected, Bharat must talk from a position of strength. Behind Xi’s swagger, after all, Beijing may be more willing to bend than it wants the world to believe.

(The writer is the author of ‘Bharat Rising: Dharma, Democracy, Diplomacy’ and ‘Eminent Distorians: Twists and Truths in Bharat’s History’. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Beyond the headcount: India’s Census needs a climate lens
editorials.passage:
India’s 2027 Census will tell us where people live, their demographic characteristics, migration histories and many aspects of their living conditions. Public discussion has understandably focused on caste enumeration, migration, representation and the questions being introduced in the new Census. One question, however, deserves more attention: what does the Census tell us about the environmental conditions in which these people live and work?

A Census is more than a headcount. It also reflects what the State considers important enough to measure. Over time, India's Census has adapted to changing priorities. Information on housing, sanitation, drinking water, cooking fuel, electricity and, more recently, digital connectivity has helped governments understand living conditions and plan public services.

India’s circumstances are changing again. Heatwaves, floods, droughts, erratic rainfall and groundwater stress are increasingly affecting agriculture, water availability, health, livelihoods and migration. These changes are being experienced not as abstract climate statistics, but in villages where wells run dry, farms become harder to cultivate, and seasonal migration becomes a necessity.

This brings us to a less discussed question: can demographic information fully serve development planning when the environmental conditions around those populations are changing so rapidly?

India already collects a great deal of relevant information. The Census, agricultural surveys, meteorological observations, groundwater assessments, disaster records and other government systems together contain a vast amount of demographic and environmental data. Yet much of this information sits in separate databases and institutions. We may know the number of households in a village and the amenities available to them, while having a much less integrated picture of the water, land and climate pressures affecting those households.

Consider two villages with roughly the same population, housing conditions and access to basic services. One is facing declining groundwater and repeated drought; the other has functioning ponds, more reliable water sources and diversified livelihoods. In a demographic table they may look similar. For a district administration deciding where to invest in water security, livelihood support or disaster preparedness, they are not.

The Census already gives us useful information about houses, drinking-water sources, sanitation, electricity, cooking fuel and other amenities. What it does not tell us, by itself, is whether a traditional water source is still functioning, whether common grazing land has declined, whether cropping patterns are changing or whether people are leaving because a local livelihood is becoming less viable.
These are questions of development as much as they are questions of the environment.

There is an intriguing precedent in India's administrative history. An 1887 village survey questionnaire from Marwar, prepared by the Mahkama Khas while compiling village histories, recorded far more than population and occupations. It asked about wells and tanks, water quality, soils, grazing lands, trees, livestock and breeds, crops, village industries, famines, epidemics, migration, local customs and community institutions.

Its purpose was administrative, not environmental in today's sense, and there is little reason to romanticise the system that produced it. Yet the questionnaire captured something important: a village was understood through both its people and the resources that sustained them.

Similar records were produced elsewhere in India through district gazetteers, settlement reports and village documentation. Rainfall, agriculture, soils, forests, irrigation, livestock and occupations often appeared alongside demographic information. The categories and purposes varied, but the underlying practical lesson was useful: a settlement cannot be understood entirely apart from its physical setting.

Today we have much better tools. Satellite imagery, remote sensing, geographic information systems, hydrological monitoring and digital databases can tell us far more about environmental change than was possible a century ago. The challenge is to bring some of this information together with demographic data in forms useful for public decision-making.

The Census questionnaire itself may not need to become much larger. The greater opportunity lies in connecting Census geography with information already collected on climate hazards, water stress, land-use change, ecological resources and livelihoods. Where reliable local information exists, it could be linked to demographic data rather than collected again through the Census.
This would make a practical difference. A district could identify villages where a large vulnerable population coincides with severe heat exposure. It could distinguish agricultural communities facing groundwater stress from those with more secure water resources. It could see where recurring floods overlap with vulnerable housing or where livelihood changes are accompanied by increasing migration.

The value of such information is not in producing another database. It is in helping administrators see relationships that are otherwise hidden when demographic and environmental information are examined separately.
Other countries are beginning to move in this direction. Uganda's 2024 Population and Housing Census included community-level questions on climate change, changing rainfall and temperature, disasters and early-warning systems. Canada has developed a Census of Environment that brings ecological information together with social and economic data. The approaches are different, but the message is similar: population statistics cannot remain completely detached from environmental change.

India does not need to copy either model. Its ecological diversity, scale and federal structure demand an approach of its own. But the broader principle is worth considering as Census 2027 takes shape.

The future of Census data may lie less in asking more questions and more in connecting the right information.

This matters because climate adaptation is ultimately local. Decisions about drinking water, drought preparedness, flood resilience, livelihood diversification and ecosystem restoration are made in particular villages, towns and neighbourhoods. National averages can tell us where problems are widespread; they cannot always tell us which community needs what kind of response.

A climate lens would therefore not turn the Census into an environmental survey. It would make demographic information more useful by placing it alongside the environmental realities that increasingly shape people's lives.

The question before Census 2027 is consequently larger than the size of its questionnaire. It is about whether the information India collects today will remain useful for the problems governments will have to address tomorrow.

Climate change is altering the relationship between people and the natural systems that sustain them. If the Census is meant to help us understand India, that changing relationship cannot remain entirely outside the frame.

Ultimately, every Census is remembered not only for the people it counted, but also for the questions it considered worth asking.

(The authors are environmental scientists and educators with over 15 years of experience. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the authors. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: The viral elephant video may be old, but the empathy it inspires is real
editorials.passage:
The video of a herd of elephants that were washed up in Uttar Pradesh after Nepal’s devastating mud flood this week has gone viral on social media. While one section claims it is recent, others say the incident happened last year, and the elephants rescued in the state have nothing to do with the current crisis in Nepal. Be that as it may, the real issue is something else.

Amid all the heartbreak and horror of what’s unfolding in Nepal, the elephant story was a rare positive and heartwarming nugget. Most people who reposted the story on various social media platforms — including me — did so because it seemed like a genuine silver lining in an unremittingly grey news landscape. There were so many headlines about the lives lost or people missing that a herd of elephants swimming to safety seemed like a genuinely feel-good story to hold on to.

This brings me to the reason why so many animal stories and videos go viral these days. With wars and worries dominating not just social media but all types of media content, the simple, heart-warming visuals of someone offering water to a monkey or a tiger sleeping in the sun or a train waiting for a herd of elephants to cross over shine bright like a real ray of hope. It makes one smile, feel good about being human, and reassured that all is not ill with the world. Even for those who do not or cannot make a material difference through charitable donations or voluntary work, just watching and sharing animal videos feels like a personal contribution.

What helps is that many Indian Forest Service officials now routinely share animal rescue videos online, highlighting the work done by their colleagues on the ground. What this has done is shine the spotlight on people who were nameless and faceless for the longest time. Just like our armed forces have a huge fan following online for doing the tough job of keeping our borders safe while we sleep peacefully at night, so do our forest rangers, who keep our endangered animals safe from human and natural dangers. The gruesome stories that highlight the incredible cruelty with which human beings treat animals in general make this category of content stand out.

What has helped these videos gain traction is a growing tribe of people genuinely interested in India’s flora and fauna. There are a whole group of wildlife photographers — many with a fan following on social media as well — who capture wild animals in their natural habitat and share those pictures online. Once again, those pictures serve a dual purpose. They offer people a glimpse into our reserve forests — important for those who are either unable to travel for some reason or, like me, are unlucky in their safari sightings. But more importantly, they normalise the idea that wild animals deserve compassion and respect. They have a right to live too.

Given the generally negative connotation of words like ‘animal’ and ‘beast’, this compassion is critical to building public opinion in favour of animal conservation. Without it, people would not care if an elephant lived or died, if a tiger was hunted down by poachers, if rhino cubs drowned in the floodwaters, or leopards were trapped and killed for their skins. Two years ago, the horrific news of a pregnant elephant getting killed with scalding iron rods made headlines all over India. Man-animal conflicts in villages bordering forest areas are not new. What’s new is the public opinion that headlines like these help build pressure on the authorities to come up with workable solutions to save both human and animal lives.

Animals, both wild and stray, suffer terribly during natural disasters. As an animal lover myself, I have routinely contributed small amounts towards rescue and rehabilitation during the floods in Assam, the 2024 Wayanad landslides or the 2025 Montha cyclone in Bengal. Earlier, this effort was mostly handled by small groups of animal lovers and private organisations. Increasingly, though, official agencies are taking over, allowing private groups to chip in wherever possible. In Assam, for example, the state’s animal husbandry and veterinary department is already running medical camps for more than 10,000 rescued farm, pet, wild and stray animals. In Kaziranga, the Centre of Wildlife Rehabilitation and Conservation has been working in collaboration with the Assam forest department to rescue and rehabilitate stranded wild animals.

Coming back to the viral elephant herd, the story is important not only because it allows us to feel empathy for them. It is also important because it lauds the efforts of those handful of people working tirelessly to rescue and rehabilitate animals. Their efforts — once they are shared and go viral — stop being fringe. A viral post brings empathy for animals mainstream rather than a rare exception. That’s how a reel can make a difference – by normalising empathy for the animal world. And in a newsroom dominated by things going wrong, that’s a rare positive story.

(Nandini Sen Gupta is a freelance writer and author of several books. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: After Nepal Floods, a Himalayan Warning: Are India's Mountain States Prepared?
editorials.passage: The first lesson from the catastrophe in Nepal’s Rasuwa district is also the most uncomfortable: the Himalaya does not recognise political borders.On the morning of 26 August, a large mass of ice and rock appears to have broken away high in the Himalaya near the Nepal-Tibet-China border.Satellite imagery indicates a substantial collapse associated with the Langtang Lirung area, while geological analysis points to the failure of both glacier material and underlying bedrock. The resulting mass entered the Lhende Khola system and generated a violent mixture of water, ice, mud, rock and sediment that travelled downstream through the Bhote Koshi and ultimately the Trishuli river system wiping out villages, homes, roads, and bridges. Nepal Death Toll Rises to 469, Hundreds Missing as Flood Threat Still LoomsNepal death toll has risen to 469, while more than 1,000 remained missing. The numbers are changing rapidly as more dead bodies are being recovered from the debris. The MEA also said on 27 August that 288 Indian nationals were still unreachable, including 73 working on the Trishuli-1 power project and several groups of Kailash Mansarovar pilgrims. The chain of events is still being investigated. The emerging evidence, however, points towards an ice-rock avalanche or glacier collapse rather than allowing us to confidently label the event a conventional Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF).For those of us who come from the Himalayas, mountains are never just mountains. They are roads we travel, rivers we cross, forests we depend on and slopes we learn to read almost instinctively. I come from Jammu and Kashmir, in the western Himalaya and have spent years writing about what happens when extreme weather collides with fragile terrain and expanding infrastructure. So, watching the devastation in Nepal does not feel like witnessing a distant disaster. The images carry a particular familiarity of the Chasoti Cloud Burst in Kishtwar. They have already shown how quickly a mountain landscape can turn dangerous.That is precisely why Nepal’s disaster deserves to be examined not simply as another Himalayan flood, but as a warning about how little we understand and how poorly we monitor and develop a rapidly changing mountain system.Nepal Floods: China’s Tibet Grip Leaves a Dangerous Information Gap in HimalayasThe Himalayas contains more than 63,700 glaciers. Yet monitoring remains sparse and uneven across the region.The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) Regional Cryosphere Strategy, released in August 2026. makes the problem explicit despite the enormous number of glaciers, only 18 percent of the 38 glaciers currently monitored meet the World Glacier Monitoring Services benchmark standards. Major glacierised areas remain poorly monitored, meaning that even where data exist, they do not necessarily provide a collective picture of how the regional cryosphere is changing. GLOFs have rightly become a major concern across the Hindu Kush Himalaya. But the danger is larger than glacial lakes themselves.ICIMOD’s latest assessment says the rate of glacier ice loss across the Hindu Kush Himalaya has doubled since 2000, while the region’s glaciers have lost as much as 27 metres of ice thickness since 1975. This is why calling the Himalaya merely a “fragile ecosystem” is no longer sufficient. It is a dynamic geological and climatic system undergoing rapid change. And our monitoring systems must reflect that reality.Nepal is not an isolated Himalayan exception. The same combination of warming, glacier retreat, unstable slopes, changing precipitation, permafrost degradation, extreme rainfall and expanding infrastructure exists across the Indian Himalaya.Just over a year ago, the Himalaya gave Jammu and Kashmir its own brutal warning. On 14 August, 2025, a cloudburst struck Chasoti in Kishtwar district, near the route to the Machail Mata shrine. Flash floods tore through the settlement, killing at least 65 people and injuring more than 100.The disaster was different from Nepal’s event. There is no reason to artificially connect the two through the same immediate trigger. But the underlying lesson is strikingly similar.In both cases, people were concentrated in narrow Himalayan valleys where extreme water and debris can move with terrifying speed. Connectivity was vulnerable. Settlements and infrastructure occupied exposed terrain. And once the event began, the geography itself made rescue difficult.Other catastrophic examples include, Chamoli, Uttarakhand, 2021, rock-and-ice avalanche followed by a devastating debris flow. South Lhonak, Sikkim, 2023,  A GLOF destroyed infrastructure and severely damaged the Teesta basin.India was already monitoring hundreds of glacial lakes through satellite observations. Government data submitted to Parliament showed that from 2022, 902 glacial lakes and water bodies were being monitored using remote sensing, including 544 glacial lakes larger than 10 hectares. Yet South Lhonak did not have an operational early-warning system when it burst. A water-level sensor installed in 2016 had failed after six months because of extreme conditions at high altitude.That should force a difficult question. If a lake is identified as potentially dangerous but the monitoring instrument cannot reliably survive where the danger exists, what exactly are we monitoring?The Himalayas function as one interconnected geological and hydrological system, but our understanding of it remains divided along national boundaries.Glaciers, rivers, slopes, snow, and permafrost do not stop at borders. A collapse or sudden release of water high in one country can become a disaster downstream in another. That raises a fundamental question: If the physical system is interconnected, why are we still monitoring it largely as separate national territories? The answer cannot simply be more data within individual countries. What the region needs is compatible, continuously updated and shareable information. The communities living closest to the Himalayan hazards are often among those who have contributed the least to the greenhouse-gas emissions driving global warming.Yet they are increasingly confronting climate disasters. For millions of mountain residents, climate change is not an abstract projection for 2050. It is already altering the landscape around them. The Hindu Kush Himalaya is home to more than 270 million people, while its river basins serve more than two billion people downstream. That makes the fate of Himalayan communities a global climate issue, not merely a regional one.There is another uncomfortable question. How much infrastructure are we placing inside a landscape whose physical behaviour is changing faster than our risk maps? Nepal’s latest disaster damaged at least 13 hydropower projects, including eight operational projects with a combined capacity of 354 MW and five under construction. This does not mean hydropower itself caused the disaster. It means something more basic: infrastructure has become deeply embedded in the pathways through which Himalayan hazards move.The same concern applies across India. Development is necessary, mountain communities need roads, electricity, communications and livelihoods.But development cannot begin with the assumption that a mountain is simply empty land waiting to be engineered. A glacier is not a reservoir waiting to be measured. A river is not merely a channel waiting to carry a project. A slope is not stable simply because it has remained standing for decades. And the Himalaya is certainly not a blank slate.Perhaps the most important question raised by the Nepal disaster concerns information. The data problem is not hypothetical. India has already experienced what happens when information across Himalayan borders becomes uncertain. An RTI response from the Ministry of Jal Shakti revealed in 2025 that China had shared no hydrological data or information on hydro structures with India since 2022. The bilateral arrangement for Brahmaputra data, intended to help India with flood forecasting, expired in June 2023 and has not been renewed. If a potentially catastrophic event originates on one side of a political boundary and its consequences arrive downstream on another, who sees the warning first? Who owns the satellite data? Who monitors the glacier?Who monitors the unstable slope? Who measures river levels? Who decides when an alert becomes an evacuation order? And, most importantly, how quickly is that information shared across borders?The Himalayas stretches across eight countries, while its rivers connect populations and infrastructure far beyond national boundaries. A hazard developing in one country can become a disaster in another within minutes or hours. Regional scientific cooperation therefore cannot remain limited to conferences, reports and post-disaster assessments.We need systems capable of sharing near-real-time information on high-risk glacial lakes, glacier movement, unstable slopes, extreme rainfall, river levels and emerging blockages.But geopolitics is only one part of the problem. In 2023, when the South Lhonak glacial lake burst in Sikkim, India already knew the lake posed a risk. Yet a water-level sensor installed there had failed after roughly six months in the extreme high-altitude environment. The disaster exposed a different vulnerability: we can identify hazards and still fail to receive the information needed to act on them.In such a landscape, when the event begins across a national boundary, monitoring cannot remain confined to individual hazards or national jurisdictions.Thus, Nepal’s tragedy must not become another disaster story that fades when the rescue ends. We need shared data, stronger monitoring, reliable early warnings, and development that respects the limits of the terrain. (Kanwal Singh is a writer and political analyst. editorials.title: Haryanvi Is Part of Delhi’s History. So Why Is It Missing From Its Identity?
editorials.passage: “In the region of Hariyanau which has numerous villages, and whose inhabitants are ever happy, there is the large city called Dhilli, favoured by Indra, destroying hostile armies, a mass of wealth, boiling the blood of the enemy.” This is how Delhi is described in 1132 by the Agravala Digambara poet Shridhar in his hagiography of the 23rd Jain Tirthankara Parshvanath, as one of the big cities of the "Haryana region".In the beginning of the 20th century, the British official George Grierson, in his Linguistic Survey of India (1916), mentions a single language spoken in the districts of Delhi, Rohtak, Karnal, and Hisar, along with the South East corner of the state of Patiala (present day Narwana).The Hariana tract at this time referred to the tehsils of Hissar, Fatehabad, and Hansi, and the eastern part of Bhiwani tehsil. The language, what is today called 'Haryanvi', was known as Jatu in Delhi and Rohtak due to the bulk population of Jats speaking the language in Hariani, Deswali or Desari in the Hariana tract. It was also called Bangaru language in Karnal and Narwana. The survey returned 2.36 lakh speakers of the language from Delhi district. Geographically, Yamuna is the eastern boundary of the Haryanvi language, hence the Haryanvi-speaking region occupies the majority area west of Yamuna in Delhi. Haryanvi-speaking villages fall in the North, North West, West, South West and Southern parts of Delhi, along with many villages of what is now marked as ‘New Delhi’ in district classifications.The area is simply a continuation of the Sonipat-Rohtak-North Jhajjar linguistic belt, coexisting with the power concentration in areas like Shahjahanabad where Urdu was the native language. Similar situations existed in other power centres, be it Agra, where Urdu was spoken by the townsmen, while others spoke Braj Bhasha.The Politics of Language in India: A Battle of Identity and PowerGrierson for this very reason separates ‘Delhi City’ and ‘Delhi Mufassil’, where the city had a Urdu speaking population, while the Mufassil was of Haryanvi majority. Even many Muslims of Karnal city and some villages are reported to speak Urdu, while the majority spoke Haryanvi.The separation of Delhi District as a territory from this contiguous region as it acquired capital status, and the creation of the state of Haryana out of the other districts speaking the language began a saga of confusion. The language became singularly known as Haryanvi and became associated with the boundaries of the modern Haryana state. While Urdu, Hindi and Punjabi became official languages of Delhi, Haryanvi was nowhere to be found.The language today is in a peculiar situation in Delhi. There is a growing number of children who are not learning Haryanvi from their parents in their formative years, as parents fear the language is unsuitable to be taught. There was a proposal to create a Haryanvi Academy in a similar fashion to the Bhojpuri-Maithili and Garhwali-Kumaoni-Jaunsari academy, but no action was taken. People think that Haryanvi speakers have come from Haryana, and some are surprised to see the existence of Haryanvi speaking villages of Delhi. People confuse sites of the powers bygone with the totality of the erstwhile ‘Delhi District’.Without revitalisation and recognition, Haryanvi will be forgotten in Delhi. My mother, who studied till Class 10, and my father, who studied till Class 8, made sure I learnt English and spoke “proper” standard Hindi. Haryanvi, the language of my village Devli in South Delhi, was not encouraged. Hauz Khaz, Mehrauli, Burari, Dhaka: The Villages That Delhi Swallowed UpI remember once saying, “कि त जावेह?” (Ki ta javeh?) meaning “Where are you going?” to my cousin. My mother immediately scolded me, saying they were wasting their hard-earned money on my education. I do not see this as their fault. It was the mirror of a society that had taught them to see their own language as a burden. For Delhi’s villages, education meant distance from Haryanvi. Standard Hindi brings respectability while speaking English is the ultimate ladder to be seen as success.This article has inputs from Akshay Kumar, who runs the project Bhashakosh, documenting the regional languages, cultures, and geographies of India.(Puneet Singh Singhal is the Founder/Curator of Dilli Dehat Project, a community-led archive and storytelling initiative that documents the rural histories, cultures, and lived realities of Delhi’s villages.
